questions.q: What are the main components of Power BI (Desktop, Service, Report Server, Mobile) and when do you use each?
questions.a: Desktop is the free authoring tool for models and reports; Service is the cloud platform for sharing, refresh, apps, and governance; Report Server is on-premises hosting for restricted environments; Mobile is the consumption app. Author in Desktop, deploy and manage in Service.

questions.q: Explain the difference between Import, DirectQuery, Dual, and Live Connection storage modes. What are the trade-offs of each?
questions.a: Import copies compressed data into VertiPaq — fastest queries, needs refresh. DirectQuery leaves data at source — real-time but slower and feature-limited. Dual lets a table act as either depending on the query. Live Connection points to an existing model (AAS/Power BI dataset) with no local model. Trade-off: performance vs freshness vs data volume.

questions.q: What is a composite model and when would you use one?
questions.a: A composite model mixes Import and DirectQuery sources (or extends a live-connected dataset with local tables) in one model. Use it to blend a large DirectQuery fact with imported dimensions, or to add local data to a certified enterprise model.

questions.q: Walk through the difference between a dataset (semantic model), a report, a dashboard, and an app in the Power BI Service.
questions.a: A semantic model holds tables, relationships, and measures; a report is a multi-page visual layer bound to one model; a dashboard pins tiles from multiple reports for at-a-glance monitoring; an app packages workspaces content for distribution to audiences.

questions.q: What is the VertiPaq engine and how does its columnar compression work? Why does cardinality matter for model size?
questions.a: VertiPaq is the in-memory columnar engine: each column is encoded (value/dictionary/RLE) and compressed independently. Compression depends on distinct values, so high-cardinality columns (IDs, timestamps) inflate model size — reduce cardinality (split datetime, remove keys) to shrink models.

questions.q: What is Power Query (M) and how does it differ from DAX? Where does each execute?
questions.a: Power Query (M) shapes data before load — extraction, cleaning, joins; it runs at refresh time. DAX defines calculations evaluated at query time inside the model. Rule of thumb: transform as upstream as possible (source/M), calculate business logic in DAX measures.

questions.q: What is query folding, why is it important, and how do you check whether a step folds?
questions.a: Query folding pushes M steps back to the source as native SQL, so filtering and joins happen in the database instead of the mashup engine — critical for refresh performance and required for incremental refresh. Check via right-click 'View native query' or query diagnostics; steps like adding index columns break folding.

questions.q: How do you design a star schema in Power BI? Why is a star schema preferred over a flat table or snowflake?
questions.a: Model facts at the correct grain in the center, one dimension table per entity, single-direction 1:many relationships from dimensions to facts. Star schemas give predictable filter propagation, simpler DAX, and better VertiPaq performance; flat tables bloat cardinality and snowflakes add join hops and complexity.

questions.q: What is the difference between a fact table and a dimension table? Give examples of degenerate and junk dimensions.
questions.a: Facts hold events/measurements at a declared grain (order lines, shipments); dimensions hold descriptive context (customer, product, date). A degenerate dimension is an attribute like invoice number kept on the fact; a junk dimension groups miscellaneous low-cardinality flags into one table.

questions.q: How do relationships work in Power BI? Explain cardinality (1:1, 1:many, many:many) and cross-filter direction (single vs both).
questions.a: Relationships propagate filters between tables. Cardinality describes key uniqueness on each side (1:1, 1:many, many:many). Cross-filter direction controls propagation: single (dimension→fact, default and safest) or both. Filters flow along relationship paths at query time.

questions.q: What are the risks of bidirectional relationships and many-to-many relationships? How do you handle them safely?
questions.a: Bidirectional filters create ambiguity, circular paths, and performance costs; many-to-many loses guaranteed uniqueness so totals can surprise. Prefer single direction plus CROSSFILTER in specific measures, or model a proper bridge table with controlled filter direction.

questions.q: What is a bridge table and when do you need one?
questions.a: A bridge table resolves genuine many-to-many relationships (e.g., one account belongs to multiple customers) by holding the key pairs. Both entities relate 1:many into the bridge, often with one bidirectional edge or TREATAS to propagate filters correctly.

questions.q: How do you handle role-playing dimensions (e.g., Order Date vs Ship Date) in Power BI?
questions.a: Create one physical date table and multiple relationships to the fact (order date active, ship date inactive), then activate the inactive one per-measure with USERELATIONSHIP. Alternatively duplicate the date dimension when users need simultaneous independent slicing.

questions.q: Explain Row-Level Security (RLS): static vs dynamic RLS, USERPRINCIPALNAME(), and how roles are tested and assigned.
questions.a: RLS filters rows per user via DAX on roles. Static RLS hardcodes filters per role; dynamic RLS filters with USERPRINCIPALNAME() against a security/mapping table, scaling to thousands of users with one role. Test with 'View as role' in Desktop and assign members in the Service; RLS applies to viewers, not workspace editors.

questions.q: What is Object-Level Security (OLS) and how does it differ from RLS?
questions.a: OLS hides entire tables or columns from specified roles (defined via Tabular Editor), securing the metadata itself — a secured column errors rather than filters. RLS restricts rows; OLS restricts schema objects like a sensitive salary column.

questions.q: What is incremental refresh? Explain RangeStart/RangeEnd parameters, partitions, and the 'detect data changes' option.
questions.a: Incremental refresh partitions a large table by date and refreshes only recent partitions. You define RangeStart/RangeEnd parameters, filter the source on them (must fold), then set archive/refresh windows. 'Detect data changes' refreshes only partitions whose max update timestamp changed.

questions.q: What are aggregation tables and how does Power BI decide when to hit the aggregation vs the detail table?
questions.a: Aggregation tables pre-summarize facts at coarser grain (imported) over a DirectQuery detail table. The engine transparently answers queries from the agg when the query's grain and columns are covered by mappings, falling back to detail otherwise — giving speed on big data with drill-to-detail.

questions.q: What is the difference between calculated columns, calculated tables, and measures? When is each appropriate, and what are the memory implications?
questions.a: Calculated columns are computed row-by-row at refresh and stored (consume memory, materialized); calculated tables similarly materialize DAX results; measures compute at query time in filter context and store nothing. Prefer measures for aggregations; push static columns to source/M.

questions.q: How do you optimize a slow Power BI report? Describe your end-to-end approach (Performance Analyzer, DAX Studio, model review, visual reduction).
questions.a: Measure with Performance Analyzer to find slow visuals, copy the DAX into DAX Studio for server timings (SE vs FE), inspect model with VertiPaq Analyzer for oversized columns, fix relationships/cardinality, simplify DAX (avoid iterators over facts), reduce visuals per page, and consider aggregations or Direct Lake.

questions.q: What is DAX Studio / Tabular Editor and what do you use them for (server timings, VertiPaq Analyzer, calculation groups, scripting)?
questions.a: DAX Studio runs queries with server timings and query plans, and hosts VertiPaq Analyzer for column-size diagnostics. Tabular Editor edits models at scale — calculation groups, OLS, scripting bulk measure changes, Best Practice Analyzer — beyond Desktop's UI.

questions.q: What are calculation groups and what problems do they solve?
questions.a: Calculation groups apply reusable calculation items (YTD, PY, YoY%) over any selected measure via SELECTEDMEASURE(), replacing dozens of near-duplicate time-intelligence measures with one maintainable structure. They also enable dynamic format strings.

questions.q: What are dataflows (Gen1/Gen2) and how do they differ from datasets? When would you centralize transformations in a dataflow?
questions.a: Dataflows are self-contained Power Query transformations stored in the Service (Gen2 writes to Fabric destinations), reusable across multiple datasets. Centralize shared cleansing logic in a dataflow so many models consume one certified, transformed source instead of duplicating M.

questions.q: What are deployment pipelines in Power BI and how do you promote content across Dev/Test/Prod?
questions.a: Deployment pipelines promote content through Dev → Test → Prod workspaces with compare views and deployment rules that rebind data sources/parameters per stage — enabling controlled releases instead of manual republish.

questions.q: How does Power BI integrate with Git / Azure DevOps for version control (PBIP format, TMDL)?
questions.a: PBIP saves reports/models as folder-based text files (model as TMDL), enabling real Git workflows: commit from Desktop, sync workspaces to Azure DevOps/GitHub branches, review diffs in PRs, and branch out per developer.

questions.q: What is the XMLA endpoint and what advanced scenarios does it enable?
questions.a: The XMLA endpoint exposes Premium/Fabric datasets as Analysis Services servers: connect Tabular Editor/DAX Studio, deploy models programmatically, manage partitions, run DAX/TMSL, and enable enterprise CI/CD and fine-grained refresh.

questions.q: Explain workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) and how app audiences control access.
questions.a: Admin has full control including deletion; Member can publish/share; Contributor can edit content but not manage access; Viewer is read-only. Apps add audience-level control so consumers see curated content without workspace access.

questions.q: What is a shared/certified/promoted dataset and why does endorsement matter in a large organization?
questions.a: A shared dataset is consumed by reports across workspaces ('one model, many reports'). Promotion is a self-declared quality flag; certification is centrally governed endorsement. Endorsement steers analysts to trusted models, reducing metric sprawl and duplicated logic.

questions.q: How do you implement drillthrough, drill down, and tooltips pages? How do they differ?
questions.a: Drill down navigates a hierarchy within one visual; drillthrough jumps to a detail page filtered to the selected data point; tooltip pages show a mini report page on hover. Drillthrough carries context via drillthrough filters (and optionally all filters).

questions.q: What are bookmarks and how do you use them for navigation and toggling visuals?
questions.a: Bookmarks capture report state — filters, slicers, visual visibility — and are triggered by buttons for navigation, view toggles, and reset-to-default experiences. Combine with selection pane to build tab-like interfaces.

questions.q: What are field parameters and what UX problems do they solve compared to bookmarks?
questions.a: Field parameters let users swap the dimension or measure a visual displays via slicer, generating a real parameter table — cleaner and more scalable than maintaining bookmark permutations for metric/axis switching.

questions.q: How do slicers, filters (visual/page/report level), and filter pane differ? How does slicer selection affect filter context?
questions.a: Slicers are on-canvas filters affecting the page (or synced pages); the filter pane offers visual, page, and report-level filters with more conditions and less canvas cost. All ultimately modify the filter context that measures evaluate in.

questions.q: What is the difference between a live connection to a dataset and a local model? What is 'edit data model' on a live connection (composite over Power BI datasets)?
questions.a: Live connection binds a report to a remote model with no local modeling. Composite over a Power BI dataset ('DirectQuery for PBI datasets') converts it to a local model that can add tables and measures while chaining to the enterprise model — powerful but adds a query hop.

questions.q: How do you handle large datasets that exceed Pro limits (Premium/Fabric capacities, large semantic model format)?
questions.a: Use Premium/Fabric capacity with the large semantic model format (removes the ~10 GB effective ceiling), incremental refresh, aggregations over DirectQuery, or Direct Lake in Fabric. Also reduce model size: drop columns, lower cardinality, disable auto date/time.

questions.q: What licensing options exist (Free, Pro, PPU, Premium/Fabric capacity) and what capabilities does each unlock?
questions.a: Free authors personal content; Pro enables sharing and workspace collaboration (per-user); PPU adds Premium features per-user (larger models, XMLA, more refreshes); Premium/Fabric capacity (P/F SKUs) provides dedicated compute, large models, and — at F64+ — free viewer access.

questions.q: How does scheduled refresh work? What is a gateway, and when do you need a personal vs standard (enterprise) gateway?
questions.a: Scheduled refresh re-imports data on a timetable (8/day Pro, 48 PPU/Premium). A gateway is on-prem software bridging the Service to private sources: personal is single-user Desktop-style, standard/enterprise is centrally managed with clusters for HA and multiple sources.

questions.q: What causes refresh failures most often and how do you troubleshoot them?
questions.a: Common causes: expired credentials, gateway offline or outdated, source schema changes breaking queries, timeouts on non-folding queries, and memory limits. Troubleshoot via refresh history error details, gateway logs, testing the query in Desktop, and validating folding.

questions.q: How do you implement dynamic formatting or dynamic titles based on slicer selection?
questions.a: Create a measure returning formatted text (SELECTEDVALUE + FORMAT) for titles via conditional formatting fx, or dynamic format strings (calculation groups/model measures) for value formatting that responds to selection.

questions.q: What is the difference between duplicate and reference queries in Power Query, and how does it affect refresh?
questions.a: Reference creates a query that reads another query's output, chaining logic (each reference may re-evaluate the source per load); duplicate copies the M code independently. References aid maintainability but can multiply source calls — staging via dataflows avoids this.

questions.q: How do you handle slowly changing dimensions (SCD Type 1 vs Type 2) in a Power BI model?
questions.a: Handle SCD upstream ideally; in-model, Type 1 simply overwrites attributes on refresh. Type 2 requires the source/warehouse to provide versioned rows with surrogate keys and effective dates — the fact joins on the surrogate key so history is preserved; Power BI just models the result.

questions.q: How do you model and visualize a parent-child hierarchy (e.g., org chart, chart of accounts) in Power BI?
questions.a: Use PATH functions (PATH, PATHITEM) in calculated columns to flatten the parent-child recursion into level columns, build a hierarchy from them, and handle ragged depth with ISINSCOPE-based measures.

questions.q: What are the best practices for date/calendar tables? Why should you mark a table as a date table?
questions.a: Use a dedicated date table spanning full years, one row per day, with year/month/quarter columns, related to facts on a date key. Mark it as a date table so time intelligence works on the key and Power BI trusts its completeness.

questions.q: What is auto date/time and why is it usually recommended to turn it off?
questions.a: Auto date/time silently builds a hidden date hierarchy table per date column, bloating the model and encouraging inconsistent time logic. Disable it and use a single marked date dimension instead.

questions.q: How do you implement currency conversion or unit conversion in a semantic model?
questions.a: Store rates in a table (date × currency), and convert via measures: multiply base amounts by the selected currency's rate using TREATAS/relationships at the correct grain. Decide converting at transaction vs reporting grain, and handle missing rates explicitly.

questions.q: How do you audit and document a semantic model (Best Practice Analyzer, INFO functions, external tools)?
questions.a: Run Best Practice Analyzer in Tabular Editor for rule-based auditing, use INFO/DMV queries or VertiPaq Analyzer to inventory columns and sizes, document measures with descriptions, and export documentation from model metadata (TMDL diffs in Git aid review).

questions.q: What is DirectLake mode (Fabric) and how does it differ from Import and DirectQuery?
questions.a: Direct Lake reads Delta Parquet files in OneLake directly into VertiPaq-style columnar memory on demand — Import-level speed without scheduled copy refresh. It falls back to DirectQuery when features/limits are exceeded, and 'framing' controls which data version is seen.

questions.q: How do you handle report accessibility and usability (themes, consistent formatting, tab order, alt text)?
questions.a: Use consistent themes (JSON theme files), readable contrast, alt text on visuals, logical tab order, meaningful titles, and avoid conveying meaning by color alone — improving usability for all users and meeting accessibility requirements.

questions.q: How would you design a semantic model to serve both self-service analysts and standardized executive reporting?
questions.a: Publish one certified semantic model with clean naming, folder-organized measures, and RLS; executives get curated apps/reports on it, while analysts connect via 'live connect' or Analyze in Excel for self-service — one governed truth, two consumption modes.

questions.q: Describe a time you reduced a model's size or refresh time significantly. What levers did you pull?
questions.a: Strong answers name concrete levers: removed high-cardinality columns, split datetime into date+time, replaced calculated columns with source columns, enabled incremental refresh, fixed non-folding steps, and pre-aggregated a billion-row fact — with before/after numbers.

questions.q: How do you embed Power BI content (Publish to web vs secure embed vs Power BI Embedded) and what are the security implications?
questions.a: Publish to web is anonymous public embedding — never for confidential data. Secure embed and Embed in SharePoint respect AAD auth and RLS. Power BI Embedded (APIs + capacity) serves external apps with app-owns-data tokens; security hinges on token scope and RLS.

questions.q: A stakeholder says 'the numbers are wrong' in a report. Walk through your systematic debugging process from visual to source.
questions.a: Reproduce the number, identify the visual's filter context (Performance Analyzer captures the DAX), test the measure in isolation, check slicers/filters/RLS, validate relationships (fan-out, missing keys), trace to Silver/source with SQL, and compare grain and dedup logic — communicate findings with evidence.

questions.q: What is evaluation context in DAX? Explain row context and filter context with examples.
questions.a: Evaluation context is the environment a DAX expression evaluates in. Row context is 'the current row' (calculated columns, iterators); filter context is the set of filters (slicers, visual coordinates, CALCULATE) restricting the model. Measures see only filter context unless an iterator creates row context.

questions.q: What does CALCULATE actually do? Explain context transition and filter arguments.
questions.a: CALCULATE evaluates an expression in a modified filter context: it transforms existing row contexts into equivalent filter contexts (context transition), then applies its filter arguments (overwriting same-column filters by default). It is the only function that changes filter context.

questions.q: What is context transition and when does it happen implicitly?
questions.a: Context transition converts the current row context into filter context — each column of the iterated row becomes a filter. It happens implicitly whenever a measure is referenced inside row context (measures are wrapped in CALCULATE), e.g., inside SUMX or a calculated column.

questions.q: Explain the difference between SUM and SUMX. When do you need an iterator?
questions.a: SUM aggregates a single column; SUMX iterates a table evaluating an expression per row, then sums. You need an iterator when the calculation involves row-level logic first, like SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty]*Sales[Price]).

questions.q: What are the performance implications of iterators over large tables? How do you minimize them?
questions.a: Iterators over large tables are fine when the expression is simple (storage-engine friendly) but slow when they force formula-engine work per row — nested measures with context transitions, IF/complex logic, or callbacks. Minimize by pre-computing columns upstream, simplifying expressions, and iterating smaller tables (VALUES of a dimension).

questions.q: What is the difference between ALL, ALLSELECTED, ALLEXCEPT, and REMOVEFILTERS?
questions.a: ALL removes filters from a table/column (also usable as a table function). ALLSELECTED restores the 'outer' filter context of the visual, respecting slicers. ALLEXCEPT removes all filters on a table except listed columns. REMOVEFILTERS is a clearer, filter-only alias for ALL.

questions.q: Explain FILTER vs direct boolean filter arguments in CALCULATE. Which is faster and why?
questions.a: A boolean argument like Sales[Region]="West" is sugar for FILTER(ALL(Sales[Region]), ...) — it operates on one column efficiently. Explicit FILTER over a whole table iterates every row, keeps other filters, and is slower; use boolean predicates where possible and FILTER only for row-by-row multi-column logic.

questions.q: What does KEEPFILTERS do and when do you need it?
questions.a: KEEPFILTERS intersects a CALCULATE filter with the existing filter context instead of overwriting it — so filtering to 'Red' inside a visual sliced to 'Blue' yields empty rather than switching to Red. Use it when you must respect user selections while adding conditions.

questions.q: What is the difference between VALUES, DISTINCT, and ALL on a column?
questions.a: ALL returns all values ignoring filter context (including blank row from invalid relationships); DISTINCT returns distinct visible values without the blank relationship row; VALUES returns visible values including the blank row when referential integrity is violated.

questions.q: How do RELATED and RELATEDTABLE work, and what contexts do they require?
questions.a: RELATED fetches a column value from the one-side following a many→one relationship and requires row context. RELATEDTABLE goes the other way, returning the related many-side rows for the current row (it's CALCULATETABLE, so it performs context transition).

questions.q: What does USERELATIONSHIP do? Give a role-playing dimension example.
questions.a: USERELATIONSHIP activates an inactive relationship for one calculation: CALCULATE([Sales], USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], 'Date'[Date])) computes sales by ship date while the order-date relationship stays active elsewhere.

questions.q: What is CROSSFILTER and when would you change filter direction in a measure?
questions.a: CROSSFILTER changes a relationship's filter direction (or disables it) within a calculation — e.g., enabling both-direction filtering for a distinct-count across a bridge without making the model globally bidirectional.

questions.q: Explain variables (VAR/RETURN) in DAX. How do they affect both readability and performance? When are variables evaluated?
questions.a: Variables store a value/table once, evaluated where defined (not where used), improving performance by avoiding repeated evaluation and improving readability. Key subtlety: a VAR captured before CALCULATE keeps its original context — useful for 'freeze this value' patterns.

questions.q: What is the difference between a measure and a calculated column in terms of evaluation context and storage?
questions.a: A calculated column computes once per row at refresh with row context and is stored in the model; a measure computes at query time in filter context and stores nothing. Columns are for slicing/grouping values; measures are for aggregations.

questions.q: Write and explain a year-to-date (YTD) measure. What does TOTALYTD require from the date table?
questions.a: Total YTD = TOTALYTD([Sales], 'Date'[Date]) or CALCULATE([Sales], DATESYTD('Date'[Date])). It requires a contiguous, marked date table covering full years; DATESYTD replaces the date filter with 1-Jan-through-current-max range.

questions.q: How do you compute year-over-year (YoY) growth? Compare SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, DATEADD, and PARALLELPERIOD.
questions.a: YoY% = DIVIDE([Sales] - [Sales PY], [Sales PY]) with Sales PY = CALCULATE([Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])). SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifts the selected dates back one year; DATEADD is the general shifter (any interval, handles partial periods); PARALLELPERIOD returns whole parallel periods regardless of partial selection.

questions.q: How do you build a rolling 12-month (or N-day moving average) measure?
questions.a: Rolling 12M = CALCULATE([Sales], DATESINPERIOD('Date'[Date], MAX('Date'[Date]), -12, MONTH)). For N-day averages, divide the rolling sum by distinct days in the window; anchor on MAX of date to roll from the current context's edge.

questions.q: How do time intelligence functions behave with non-standard calendars (4-4-5, fiscal years)? What alternatives exist?
questions.a: Built-in time intelligence assumes standard Gregorian calendars; 4-4-5/fiscal calendars break SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR-style logic. Alternatives: enrich the date table with fiscal period columns and write custom logic (offset columns like YearOffset/MonthOffset enable simple filter arithmetic).

questions.q: What is the difference between DATESINPERIOD and DATESBETWEEN?
questions.a: DATESINPERIOD returns a rolling window of a given length back/forward from a start date (e.g., last 12 months); DATESBETWEEN returns dates between two explicit boundary dates you compute yourself.

questions.q: How do you calculate 'sales of the last non-empty date' (semi-additive measures, e.g., inventory or account balances)?
questions.a: Use LASTNONBLANK/LASTNONBLANKVALUE or CALCULATE(SUM(Balance), LASTNONBLANK('Date'[Date], [Balance])) so period totals show the closing value instead of summing daily snapshots — the semi-additive pattern for balances and inventory.

questions.q: Explain RANKX. What are common pitfalls (ties, context, using the measure inside RANKX)?
questions.a: RANKX(ALL(Dim[Col]), [Measure]) ranks the current context's measure value against the measure evaluated over each ranked row. Pitfalls: forgetting ALL (everything ranks 1), ties defaulting to SKIP, ranking by an expression not matching the displayed measure, and blank handling.

questions.q: How does TOPN work and how do you handle ties?
questions.a: TOPN returns the top N rows of a table by an expression — typically wrapped in CALCULATE([Sales], TOPN(...)) or used for top-N visuals. Ties: TOPN returns more than N rows when boundary values tie, so handle deterministic tiebreakers (add a second sort expression).

questions.q: What is the difference between SUMMARIZE, SUMMARIZECOLUMNS, and ADDCOLUMNS+SUMMARIZE best practice?
questions.a: SUMMARIZE groups a table by columns (safe for grouping, risky for adding computed columns due to context ambiguity); ADDCOLUMNS(SUMMARIZE(...), ...) is the recommended pattern to group then compute; SUMMARIZECOLUMNS is the modern, optimized query-level function (used by visuals) but has limitations inside measures.

questions.q: What do TREATAS, INTERSECT, and virtual relationships do? When would you use TREATAS instead of a physical relationship?
questions.a: TREATAS applies a table's values as filters onto target columns without a physical relationship — powering virtual relationships (e.g., filtering by a disconnected parameter table). INTERSECT/EXCEPT do set operations on tables; TREATAS is preferred for lineage-preserving virtual filters when a physical relationship isn't possible.

questions.q: What is expanded table theory and how does it explain RELATED and filter propagation?
questions.a: Each table logically 'expands' to include all one-side related tables' columns. Filters on a table filter its expanded version — explaining why filtering a dimension filters facts, how RELATED works (reading expanded columns), and subtle behaviors of ALL on expanded tables.

questions.q: What is the difference between ISFILTERED, ISCROSSFILTERED, HASONEVALUE, HASONEFILTER, and SELECTEDVALUE?
questions.a: ISFILTERED: direct filter on a column; ISCROSSFILTERED: filtered directly or via relationships; HASONEVALUE: exactly one visible value; HASONEFILTER: exactly one directly-filtered value; SELECTEDVALUE returns the single visible value or an alternate — the standard for reading slicer selections.

questions.q: How do you write a measure that responds differently at different hierarchy levels (ISINSCOPE)?
questions.a: Use ISINSCOPE('Dim'[Level]) to detect which hierarchy level the current cell is computing at, then SWITCH logic per level — e.g., show ratios at leaf level but sums at subtotal rows.

questions.q: How do you handle division safely? DIVIDE vs the / operator.
questions.a: DIVIDE(numerator, denominator [, alternate]) handles divide-by-zero/blank safely and is optimized; the / operator raises errors on zero. Use DIVIDE everywhere denominators can be zero or blank.

questions.q: What is the difference between BLANK() and 0 in DAX? How do blanks propagate in visuals and how do you control them?
questions.a: BLANK() is absence of value: it's ignored by aggregations, rows with blank measures are hidden in visuals by default, and BLANK()=0 is TRUE in comparisons (a classic trap). Convert deliberately (COALESCE/+0) only when display requires it.

questions.q: Why can returning 0 instead of BLANK() destroy report performance on sparse data?
questions.a: Returning 0 makes the measure non-blank for every dimension combination, forcing visuals to materialize the full cross-join (e.g., every customer × every product) instead of only existing combinations — turning fast sparse scans into enormous result sets.

questions.q: Explain CALCULATETABLE vs FILTER for producing filtered tables.
questions.a: CALCULATETABLE is CALCULATE for tables: it modifies filter context (with context transition) before evaluating a table expression — efficient for applying filters. FILTER iterates row-by-row with a predicate — needed for complex per-row conditions but slower for simple filters.

questions.q: What are the storage engine (SE) and formula engine (FE) in VertiPaq? How do you identify which one is the bottleneck?
questions.a: The storage engine (VertiPaq) scans compressed columns fast and parallel; the formula engine executes the query plan single-threaded and handles complex logic. In DAX Studio server timings, high SE% with few queries is healthy; high FE time or huge SE result rows indicate the bottleneck.

questions.q: What is a CallbackDataID and why is it bad for performance?
questions.a: A CallbackDataID appears when the storage engine must call the formula engine per row (e.g., IF or error-handling inside an iterated expression) — it disables SE caching and parallel efficiency. Refactor expressions (remove IFs from tight loops, use DIVIDE, pre-compute columns) to eliminate them.

questions.q: How do you read a DAX query plan / server timings in DAX Studio?
questions.a: Focus on: total duration split FE vs SE, number of SE queries and their rows/KB returned (huge materializations are red flags), CallbackDataID presence, and repeated identical SE queries (missing cache reuse). Optimize the biggest SE materialization or FE-heavy operation first.

questions.q: What does EVALUATE do? Write a basic DAX query with DEFINE MEASURE for testing.
questions.a: EVALUATE is the DAX query statement returning a table: DEFINE MEASURE Sales[Test] = ... EVALUATE SUMMARIZECOLUMNS('Date'[Year], "Sales", [Test]) — the standard way to test measures in DAX Studio/DAX query view without touching the model.

questions.q: What are calculation groups and how do calculation items with SELECTEDMEASURE() work? What is precedence?
questions.a: Calculation items are DAX expressions applied over SELECTEDMEASURE() — e.g., a 'PY' item wraps any measure in SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR. Precedence orders application when multiple calculation groups are active; lower precedence applies first (closest to the measure).

questions.q: How do you implement dynamic measure selection (field parameters vs SWITCH-based disconnected tables)?
questions.a: Field parameters swap actual fields/measures natively in visuals with automatic axis labels — preferred for UX. SWITCH-based disconnected tables (SELECTEDVALUE driving SWITCH([A],[B],...)) offer full control including conditional formatting/logic but require writing the dispatch measure.

questions.q: How do you implement ABC/Pareto classification in DAX?
questions.a: Compute each item's cumulative share: rank items by measure, sum measure for items with rank ≤ current (via FILTER over VALUES), divide by total, then classify with IF thresholds (A ≤70%, B ≤90%, else C) — typically as a measure or a calculated column if static slicing is needed.

questions.q: How would you compute a cumulative total that works across any filter (not just dates)?
questions.a: Cumulative = CALCULATE([Measure], FILTER(ALLSELECTED(Dim[Col]), Dim[Col] <= MAX(Dim[Col]))) — works for any ordered column, not just dates, by re-filtering the dimension up to the current row's value while respecting outer selections.

questions.q: How do you calculate distinct customers who bought in both period A and period B (basket/cohort overlap)?
questions.a: Compute each period's customer set with CALCULATETABLE(VALUES(Sales[CustomerID]), period filter), then COUNTROWS(INTERSECT(setA, setB)) — table functions and set operators express basket/cohort overlap cleanly.

questions.q: How do you build a cohort retention analysis in DAX?
questions.a: Tag each customer with a cohort (first purchase month, via MINX/calculated column), then for each cohort × months-since matrix cell compute DISTINCTCOUNT of active customers divided by cohort size — using offset math on the date table for the 'months since' axis.

questions.q: What are the pitfalls of using FILTER over an entire fact table inside CALCULATE?
questions.a: FILTER over an entire fact iterates millions of rows in the formula engine, prevents efficient SE plans, and breaks filter overwrite semantics expectations. Filter dimension columns instead, or FILTER(ALL(Fact[Column]), ...) on a single column when unavoidable.

questions.q: Explain how a measure total row can differ from the sum of its parts, and how to control totals (SUMX over VALUES pattern).
questions.a: Totals are not sums of visible rows — the measure re-evaluates in the total's (broader) filter context, so MAX-style, ratio, or TOPN measures diverge naturally. To force additive totals use SUMX(VALUES(Dim[Col]), [Measure]), iterating the visual's rows explicitly.

questions.q: What is the 'measure branching' technique and why does it help maintainability?
questions.a: Measure branching builds complex measures from small named building blocks ([Sales], [Sales PY], [YoY %]) instead of monolithic expressions — enabling reuse, easier testing, single-point fixes, and consistent logic across reports.

questions.q: How do LOOKUPVALUE and RELATED differ, and why is LOOKUPVALUE often a performance smell?
questions.a: RELATED follows an existing relationship (fast, engine-optimized); LOOKUPVALUE searches a table by matching column values with no relationship needed. Frequent LOOKUPVALUE usually signals a missing relationship or modeling problem, and it's slower.

questions.q: What does GENERATE / GENERATEALL do? Give a practical use case.
questions.a: GENERATE evaluates a second table expression for each row of the first and unions results (correlated cross join); GENERATEALL keeps rows with empty results. Use for per-group top-N tables (each category with its top products) or generating parameter combinations.

questions.q: How do you debug a complex DAX measure step by step (variables returning intermediates, TOCSV/EVALUATEANDLOG, DAX query view)?
questions.a: Break the measure into VARs and return intermediates one at a time; test in DAX query view with EVALUATE and known filters; use EVALUATEANDLOG or TOCSV to inspect tables; compare against hand-computed expected values on a tiny filter; check filter context with dummy measures like COUNTROWS(VALUES(...)).

questions.q: What is the difference between ALLSELECTED and ALL in the context of visual totals? Why is ALLSELECTED considered tricky?
questions.a: ALL ignores everything including slicers; ALLSELECTED removes only the filters introduced 'inside' the visual (rows/columns) while keeping user selections — so '% of visible total' uses ALLSELECTED. It's tricky because its result depends on shadow filter contexts, behaving unexpectedly when nested in iterators.

questions.q: How do you optimize a many-to-many measure pattern over a bridge table?
questions.a: Ensure the bridge is thin (just keys), keep the dimension→bridge relationship bidirectional (or use CROSSFILTER in-measure), pre-aggregate where possible, and consider replacing the M2M with a denormalized fact key or TREATAS on a smaller intermediate table if performance suffers.

questions.q: You need a measure for '% of total by category, respecting slicers but ignoring the category filter itself' — write it and explain each function choice.
questions.a: Pct = VAR t = CALCULATE([Sales], REMOVEFILTERS(Dim[Category])) RETURN DIVIDE([Sales], t). REMOVEFILTERS clears only the category filter so slicers on other columns still apply; DIVIDE guards zero; using ALLSELECTED(Dim[Category]) instead would make the denominator respect other visuals' cross-highlighting of category.

questions.q: Explain the logical order of SQL query execution (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT) and why aliases behave the way they do.
questions.a: Logical order: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/TOP. SELECT aliases don't exist yet in WHERE/GROUP BY (they're assigned in SELECT), but ORDER BY can use them because it runs after SELECT.

questions.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
questions.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping (no aggregates allowed); HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Filter as early as possible in WHERE for performance; use HAVING only for aggregate conditions like HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000.

questions.q: Explain INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, CROSS, and SELF joins with use cases.
questions.a: INNER returns only matches; LEFT keeps all left rows with NULLs for non-matches (find-missing patterns); RIGHT mirrors it; FULL OUTER keeps both sides; CROSS produces the Cartesian product (date scaffolds); SELF joins a table to itself (employees to managers, row-to-previous-row pre-window-functions).

questions.q: What happens to row counts when you join on a non-unique key? How do you detect and handle join fan-out (duplication)?
questions.a: Joining on a non-unique key multiplies rows (fan-out): each left row repeats per matching right row, inflating aggregates. Detect by comparing pre/post counts or GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*)>1 on the join key; fix by deduplicating/aggregating the many-side to the join grain first.

questions.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and the performance implication?
questions.a: UNION removes duplicates (implicit sort/hash — expensive); UNION ALL simply appends. Default to UNION ALL unless dedup is a requirement; both need matching column counts and compatible types.

questions.q: What are INTERSECT and EXCEPT and when are they cleaner than joins?
questions.a: INTERSECT returns rows in both sets; EXCEPT returns rows in the first not the second — both dedup and treat NULLs as equal, making 'what's missing between tables' cleaner and safer than LEFT JOIN...IS NULL with NULLable keys.

questions.q: What is the difference between DISTINCT and GROUP BY for deduplication?
questions.a: Both can dedup, but DISTINCT applies to the selected row as a whole while GROUP BY defines groups you can aggregate over. Use GROUP BY when you need aggregates; use DISTINCT for simple uniqueness. Performance is typically equivalent — same plan.

questions.q: Explain window functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE. How do they differ on ties?
questions.a: Window functions compute over a partition without collapsing rows. ROW_NUMBER gives unique sequence (ties broken arbitrarily); RANK leaves gaps after ties (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK doesn't (1,1,2); NTILE(n) splits rows into n near-equal buckets.

questions.q: Explain LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, and window frames (ROWS BETWEEN vs RANGE BETWEEN).
questions.a: LAG/LEAD read previous/next row values within a partition ordering; FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE read frame edges — LAST_VALUE needs ROWS BETWEEN ... AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING because the default frame ends at the current row. ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE groups peers with equal ORDER BY values.

questions.q: How do you compute a running total and a moving average with window functions?
questions.a: Running total: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY dt ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING). Moving average: AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY dt ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) for a 7-row window.

questions.q: What is the difference between PARTITION BY and GROUP BY?
questions.a: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group; PARTITION BY defines groups for a window calculation while keeping every row. Use windows when you need detail rows alongside group-level values (share of group, running totals, rankings).

questions.q: Write a query to find the second-highest salary (multiple approaches) and discuss trade-offs.
questions.a: Approaches: SELECT MAX(sal) WHERE sal < (SELECT MAX(sal)); OFFSET 1 FETCH 1 after ORDER BY DESC; DENSE_RANK()=2 in a CTE. DENSE_RANK generalizes to Nth and handles ties correctly; OFFSET is simplest but tie behavior depends on requirement.

questions.q: How do you deduplicate rows keeping the latest record per key (ROW_NUMBER pattern)?
questions.a: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn in a CTE, then WHERE rn = 1 — the canonical latest-record-per-key pattern; QUALIFY shortens it on engines that support it.

questions.q: What are CTEs? How do they compare to subqueries and temp tables for readability and performance?
questions.a: CTEs (WITH) name subqueries for readable, composable steps and enable recursion. Vs subqueries: same performance usually (inlined), better readability. Vs temp tables: temp tables materialize once with stats — better when reused many times or when the optimizer mis-estimates a complex CTE.

questions.q: Explain recursive CTEs with an example (org hierarchy, date series).
questions.a: A recursive CTE has an anchor member UNION ALL a recursive member referencing itself, iterating until empty — e.g., walking manager_id chains to build org paths/levels, or generating a continuous date series between two dates.

questions.q: What is a correlated subquery and why can it be slow? How would you rewrite one as a join?
questions.a: A correlated subquery references outer-query columns, so it logically executes per outer row — often O(n×m). Rewrite as a JOIN to a pre-aggregated derived table (GROUP BY the correlation key) or a window function, letting the engine hash/merge once.

questions.q: What is the difference between EXISTS, IN, and JOIN for semi-joins? How do they treat NULLs (especially NOT IN)?
questions.a: EXISTS short-circuits on first match and handles NULLs sanely — preferred for semi-joins. IN is fine for small lists but NOT IN returns zero rows if the subquery yields any NULL (three-valued logic trap) — use NOT EXISTS. JOIN risks row duplication when used just to filter.

questions.q: How does NULL behave in comparisons, aggregations, GROUP BY, and joins? What do COALESCE and NULLIF do?
questions.a: NULL compares as UNKNOWN (use IS NULL, not = NULL); aggregates ignore NULLs (COUNT(col) skips them); GROUP BY treats NULLs as one group; joins never match NULL keys. COALESCE returns first non-null; NULLIF(a,b) returns NULL when a=b — handy to avoid divide-by-zero.

questions.q: Explain the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column), and COUNT(DISTINCT column).
questions.a: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts rows where col is non-null; COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-null values (more expensive — requires dedup). Differences between them are a quick data-quality signal for null density.

questions.q: What are GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, and CUBE?
questions.a: They compute multiple grouping levels in one pass: GROUPING SETS lists explicit combinations; ROLLUP produces hierarchical subtotals (a,b → a → grand total); CUBE produces all combinations. GROUPING() identifies subtotal rows.

questions.q: How do you pivot and unpivot data in SQL (PIVOT operator vs conditional aggregation)?
questions.a: Conditional aggregation pivots portably: SUM(CASE WHEN month='Jan' THEN amt END) per column; the PIVOT operator does it declaratively on SQL Server. Unpivot via UNPIVOT or CROSS APPLY (VALUES ...) to rotate columns into rows.

questions.q: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP?
questions.a: DELETE removes rows (logged per-row, WHERE-able, triggers fire, rollback-friendly); TRUNCATE deallocates all pages (fast, minimal logging, resets identity, no WHERE); DROP removes the object entirely including structure.

questions.q: Explain primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints, and check constraints. How do they support data quality?
questions.a: Primary keys enforce unique, non-null row identity; foreign keys enforce referential integrity to a parent; unique constraints enforce alternate keys; checks enforce value rules. They push data quality into the database so bad data fails loudly at write time.

questions.q: What is normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) and when do you deliberately denormalize for analytics?
questions.a: 1NF: atomic values; 2NF: no partial dependency on a composite key; 3NF: no transitive dependencies. OLTP normalizes to prevent anomalies; analytics denormalizes (star schemas, wide tables) to reduce joins and favor scan-heavy columnar engines.

questions.q: What is a surrogate key vs a natural key, and why do warehouses prefer surrogates?
questions.a: A natural key comes from business data (email, order number); a surrogate is a meaningless generated integer/hash. Warehouses prefer surrogates for stable joins despite source changes, SCD2 versioning (multiple rows per natural key), compact fact keys, and cross-source integration.

questions.q: How do clustered and non-clustered indexes work? What is a covering index?
questions.a: A clustered index defines the physical row order of the table (one per table); non-clustered indexes are separate ordered structures pointing back to rows. A covering index includes all queried columns so the engine never touches the base table, eliminating key lookups.

questions.q: How do you read an execution plan? What are seeks vs scans, and common red flags (key lookups, spills, implicit conversions)?
questions.a: Read plans right-to-left/inner-to-outer, checking estimated vs actual rows. Seeks touch selective ranges; scans read everything (fine for analytics, bad for selective OLTP queries). Red flags: massive estimate misses, key lookups on many rows, hash/sort spills to tempdb, implicit conversions killing sargability.

questions.q: What are statistics and why do stale statistics cause bad plans?
questions.a: Statistics are histograms of column value distributions the optimizer uses to estimate row counts and choose join/scan strategies. Stale stats after big loads cause wildly wrong estimates and bad plans — update statistics post-load or enable auto-update with care on large tables.

questions.q: What is parameter sniffing and how do you mitigate it?
questions.a: The engine compiles a procedure's plan using the first parameter values seen; atypical values then get a plan tuned for someone else's data. Mitigate with OPTION(RECOMPILE) on the problem statement, OPTIMIZE FOR, dynamic branching into separate procedures, or engine-specific parameter-sensitive plan features.

questions.q: What makes a predicate non-SARGable? Give examples and fixes.
questions.a: Non-SARGable predicates prevent index seeks: functions on columns (YEAR(dt)=2025), leading-wildcard LIKE ('%abc'), implicit type conversions, OR sprawl. Fix by rewriting to range predicates (dt >= '2025-01-01' AND dt < '2026-01-01'), computed/persisted columns, or matching types exactly.

questions.q: Explain ACID properties and transaction isolation levels (read uncommitted → serializable). What anomalies does each prevent?
questions.a: Atomicity: all-or-nothing; Consistency: constraints hold; Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere; Durability: commits survive crashes. Isolation levels trade anomalies for concurrency — read uncommitted allows dirty reads; read committed blocks them; repeatable read stops non-repeatable reads; serializable stops phantoms; snapshot/RCSI gives readers versioned non-blocking reads.

questions.q: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic concurrency? What are deadlocks and how do you reduce them?
questions.a: Pessimistic locking blocks conflicts up front (locks); optimistic assumes rare conflicts and validates at commit (row versions), retrying losers. Deadlocks are circular waits — reduce by consistent object access order, short transactions, appropriate indexes, and snapshot isolation to remove reader-writer blocking.

questions.q: What is MERGE (upsert) and what are its pitfalls?
questions.a: MERGE performs INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in one statement by matching source to target. Pitfalls: unexpected multi-match errors when the source isn't unique on the key, historical SQL Server bugs, concurrency race conditions without HOLDLOCK, and complex semantics — many teams prefer explicit UPDATE-then-INSERT.

questions.q: How do you implement SCD Type 2 in pure SQL (effective dates, current flag, hash compare)?
questions.a: SCD2 upsert: close changed current rows (set end_date/current_flag=0) where the natural key matches and attribute hash differs, then insert new versions with start_date=load date and current_flag=1. A hash/CHECKSUM over tracked attributes makes change detection cheap.

questions.q: How do you validate row counts and reconcile data between source and target tables in SQL?
questions.a: Reconcile at multiple levels: row counts per partition/day, SUM/hash totals of measures, distinct key counts, and EXCEPT queries to find exact mismatched rows. Automate as post-load assertions logged to an audit table with thresholds and alerting.

questions.q: Write a query to find gaps and islands in a sequence (e.g., consecutive login streaks).
questions.a: Gaps-and-islands: assign ROW_NUMBER ordered by date, then group by date minus row_number (constant within a consecutive run) — each group is an island; gaps are boundaries between islands. Used for streaks, continuous coverage, and sessionization.

questions.q: How do you calculate month-over-month change per entity using window functions?
questions.a: prev = LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY month); change = amount - prev; pct = (amount - prev) / NULLIF(prev, 0). LAG keeps it single-pass instead of self-joining to the prior month.

questions.q: How would you find customers who purchased in January but not February?
questions.a: SELECT customer_id FROM sales WHERE month='Jan' EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM sales WHERE month='Feb' — or a LEFT JOIN from January purchasers to February purchasers filtering NULLs; EXCEPT reads most clearly.

questions.q: How do you compute median and percentiles in SQL (PERCENTILE_CONT vs PERCENTILE_DISC)?
questions.a: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY val) interpolates a continuous median; PERCENTILE_DISC returns an actual existing value. On engines without them, use APPROX_PERCENTILE for scale or ROW_NUMBER/COUNT math for exact medians.

questions.q: What is the difference between a view, an indexed/materialized view, and a table? When do you materialize?
questions.a: A view is a stored query (no data, always current, can simplify/secure); an indexed/materialized view persists results for fast reads at maintenance cost; a table is fully materialized data you refresh yourself. Materialize when the computation is expensive, reused often, and freshness requirements allow.

questions.q: What are stored procedures and functions? Scalar vs table-valued functions and their performance traps.
questions.a: Procedures encapsulate multi-statement logic with parameters (ETL steps, admin tasks); scalar UDFs run per-row and historically destroy performance (pre-inlining); inline table-valued functions are parameterized views — optimizer-friendly; multi-statement TVFs hide cardinality and mislead plans. Prefer inline TVFs.

questions.q: What are temp tables vs table variables vs CTEs — how do you choose?
questions.a: Temp tables (#t) persist in tempdb with stats and indexes — best for large intermediate sets reused multiple times. Table variables have minimal stats (poor estimates historically) — fine for tiny sets. CTEs are inlined logic, re-evaluated per reference — best for readability and single-use steps.

questions.q: How do you handle string parsing in SQL (STRING_SPLIT, STRING_AGG, CHARINDEX/SUBSTRING)?
questions.a: STRING_SPLIT breaks delimited strings into rows (add ordinal where supported); STRING_AGG concatenates rows into a delimited string with ORDER BY inside WITHIN GROUP; CHARINDEX locates substrings and SUBSTRING extracts by position — combined for parsing semi-structured columns.

questions.q: How do date functions differ across engines (DATEADD/DATEDIFF, EXTRACT, date truncation)? How do you handle time zones?
questions.a: SQL Server uses DATEADD/DATEDIFF/DATETRUNC; ANSI engines use EXTRACT and INTERVAL arithmetic; truncation-to-month varies (DATETRUNC, DATE_TRUNC, EOMONTH). Store timestamps in UTC (datetimeoffset where relevant), convert at presentation with AT TIME ZONE, and never compare naive local times across regions.

questions.q: What is partitioning in large tables and how does partition elimination speed up queries?
questions.a: Partitioning splits a table by a key (usually date) into separately-stored ranges. Queries filtering the partition key touch only relevant partitions (partition elimination); loads can switch partitions in/out for near-instant archival — but it's a manageability feature more than a pure speed feature.

questions.q: What is columnstore vs rowstore storage and why do columnstores dominate analytics workloads?
questions.a: Rowstores store complete rows together — great for OLTP point lookups and updates. Columnstores store each column contiguously with heavy compression, reading only referenced columns with batch-mode execution — 10–100x for scan-and-aggregate analytics over wide tables.

questions.q: How would you optimize a query joining a billion-row fact to several dimensions? Walk through your checklist.
questions.a: Checklist: verify columnstore/partitioning on the fact; ensure predicate pushdown and partition elimination; confirm join keys are same-typed integers; check dimension sizes (broadcastable?); pre-aggregate if the query grain is coarser than fact grain; examine plan for spills and skewed distribution; update stats; consider pre-computed summary tables.

questions.q: What is dynamic SQL, when is it justified, and how do you prevent SQL injection?
questions.a: Dynamic SQL builds statements as strings for variable objects/columns — justified for metadata-driven frameworks and admin tooling. Prevent injection: parameterize with sp_executesql, never concatenate user input, whitelist identifiers via QUOTENAME, and restrict executing accounts.

questions.q: How do you test SQL transformations (unit tests, known-answer tests, assertions on grain and uniqueness)?
questions.a: Test with known-answer fixtures: small input datasets with expected outputs asserted automatically (dbt tests, tSQLt, pytest against a test DB). Always assert grain (unique keys), row-count reconciliations, null/negative checks on critical columns, and referential integrity between layers.

questions.q: You inherit a 500-line legacy query with nested subqueries that runs for 40 minutes. Describe your refactoring and optimization approach.
questions.a: Approach: capture current output on sample data as a baseline; break the monolith into CTE steps; identify the grain of each step and remove premature DISTINCTs masking join fan-out; replace correlated subqueries with window functions; check plan for scans/spills; add missing indexes or pre-aggregations; validate refactor equals baseline, then optimize iteratively with timings.

questions.q: What are Python's core data structures (list, tuple, set, dict) and their time complexities for common operations?
questions.a: Lists: ordered, mutable, O(1) append/index, O(n) membership. Tuples: immutable, hashable. Sets: unordered, unique, O(1) membership/add. Dicts: key-value, O(1) lookup/insert. Choosing the right structure (set for membership, dict for lookup) is the most common practical optimization.

questions.q: When would you use a tuple over a list, or a set over a list?
questions.a: Tuples for fixed heterogeneous records, dictionary keys, and signaling immutability. Sets when uniqueness or fast membership tests matter — deduping IDs or checking 'seen' items in loops.

questions.q: What is the difference between mutable and immutable objects, and what bugs does mutability cause (e.g., mutable default arguments)?
questions.a: Immutable: int, str, tuple, frozenset; mutable: list, dict, set. Classic bug: def f(x, acc=[]) — the default list is created once and shared across calls; use None sentinel. Also aliasing: b = a on a list makes both names point to one object.

questions.q: How does Python pass arguments — by value or by reference? Explain 'pass by object reference'.
questions.a: Python passes object references by value: reassigning a parameter doesn't affect the caller, but mutating a passed mutable object does. Understanding this explains most 'my function changed my data' surprises.

questions.q: What is the difference between == and is?
questions.a: == compares values (calls __eq__); is compares identity (same object in memory). Use is only for None/True/False singletons: x is None.

questions.q: Explain list, dict, and set comprehensions. When do they hurt readability?
questions.a: Comprehensions build collections declaratively: [x*2 for x in xs if x>0], {k: v for ...}, {x for ...}. They hurt readability when nested deeply or containing complex conditionals — switch to loops or named helper functions there.

questions.q: What are generators and the yield keyword? Why are they memory-efficient for large data processing?
questions.a: Generators produce values lazily via yield, holding only current state instead of a full collection — so you can stream a 100 GB file line-by-line in constant memory. Generator expressions (sum(x for x in ...)) avoid intermediate lists.

questions.q: What is the difference between an iterable, an iterator, and a generator?
questions.a: An iterable can produce an iterator (has __iter__); an iterator yields items via __next__ and is exhausted once consumed; a generator is an iterator created by a function with yield (or a genexp). Files, ranges, and DataFrame chunks are all iterables you loop lazily.

questions.q: What are *args and **kwargs and when do you use them?
questions.a: *args collects extra positional arguments as a tuple; **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments as a dict. Use for flexible wrappers, decorators, and passing options through to underlying libraries (e.g., forwarding read_csv kwargs).

questions.q: What are lambda functions and where are they appropriate (sorted key, map/filter) vs discouraged?
questions.a: Lambdas are anonymous single-expression functions — appropriate as short keys: sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r['date']). Discouraged when logic grows, needs a name for testing, or is assigned to a variable (just def it).

questions.q: Explain shallow copy vs deep copy.
questions.a: Shallow copy (copy.copy, list slicing, dict.copy) duplicates the container but shares nested objects; deep copy (copy.deepcopy) recursively duplicates everything. Nested config dicts modified after shallow copy are a classic pipeline bug.

questions.q: What are decorators? Write a simple timing or retry decorator and explain how it works.
questions.a: A decorator wraps a function to extend behavior: def retry(fn): @wraps(fn) def inner(*a, **k): for attempt in range(3): try: return fn(*a,**k) except Exception: sleep(2**attempt) return inner. Applied with @retry — cross-cutting concerns (timing, retries, logging) without touching business logic.

questions.q: What are context managers and the with statement? Why do they matter for files and DB connections?
questions.a: Context managers guarantee setup/teardown via __enter__/__exit__: with open(path) as f, or with engine.connect() as conn. They release files, connections, and locks even when exceptions occur — essential to avoid leaked handles in long-running pipelines.

questions.q: How does Python handle exceptions? Explain try/except/else/finally and creating custom exceptions.
questions.a: try runs risky code; except catches specific exception types (narrowest first); else runs when no exception occurred; finally always runs (cleanup). Custom exceptions (class DataQualityError(Exception)) let callers distinguish pipeline failure modes.

questions.q: What is the difference between raising and catching exceptions in a data pipeline — when should a pipeline fail fast vs log and continue?
questions.a: Fail fast on structural problems (missing source, schema break, credentials) — continuing produces garbage. Log-and-continue (with quarantine) for isolated bad records when partial delivery is acceptable and tracked. The decision should be explicit per error class, with counts surfaced to monitoring either way.

questions.q: Explain Python's GIL. What does it mean for multithreading vs multiprocessing in data workloads?
questions.a: The Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, so threads don't parallelize CPU-bound pure-Python work. Threads still help I/O-bound tasks (waiting releases the GIL); CPU parallelism needs multiprocessing or GIL-releasing native libraries (NumPy, Polars).

questions.q: When would you choose multiprocessing, threading, or asyncio for a data task (I/O-bound vs CPU-bound)?
questions.a: CPU-bound (parsing, computation): multiprocessing or vectorized libraries. I/O-bound with moderate concurrency (a few API calls, DB queries): threading. I/O-bound with high concurrency (hundreds of requests): asyncio. Measure first — most 'slow Python' in data work is fixed by vectorization, not concurrency.

questions.q: How does Python manage memory (reference counting, garbage collection)? What are common causes of memory leaks in long-running jobs?
questions.a: CPython uses reference counting (objects freed when count hits zero) plus a cyclic garbage collector for reference cycles. Long-running job leaks typically come from unbounded caches/dicts, accumulating global lists, holding DataFrame references, or C-extension leaks — profile with tracemalloc.

questions.q: What are type hints and tools like mypy/pydantic? Why do they matter in production pipelines?
questions.a: Type hints (def load(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame) document intent and let mypy catch type bugs pre-runtime; pydantic validates data at runtime (API payloads, configs) with typed models. In pipelines they turn silent data-shape errors into loud, early failures.

questions.q: What is the difference between a module and a package? How do imports and __init__.py work?
questions.a: A module is a .py file; a package is a directory of modules with __init__.py. Imports resolve via sys.path; absolute imports (from myproj.utils import x) are preferred. Import-time side effects and circular imports are the common traps.

questions.q: How do virtual environments work (venv, conda, poetry/uv)? Why are pinned dependencies critical for reproducible pipelines?
questions.a: Virtual environments isolate per-project dependencies (venv/conda/poetry/uv). Pinned lockfiles guarantee the exact versions in prod match dev — unpinned dependencies are a top cause of 'worked yesterday' pipeline failures, e.g., a pandas minor release changing behavior.

questions.q: What is if __name__ == '__main__' and why is it used?
questions.a: It distinguishes 'run as a script' from 'imported as a module': the guarded block executes only when run directly. It keeps imports side-effect-free — critical for tests, multiprocessing on Windows, and orchestrators importing your module.

questions.q: Explain OOP basics in Python: classes, inheritance, composition, dunder methods (__init__, __repr__, __eq__).
questions.a: Classes bundle state and behavior (__init__ constructor, self instance state); inheritance shares/overrides behavior; composition (has-a) is usually preferable to deep inheritance. __repr__ aids debugging; __eq__ defines equality semantics for comparisons and tests.

questions.q: What are dataclasses and when are they better than dicts or plain classes for pipeline records/configs?
questions.a: Dataclasses auto-generate __init__/__repr__/__eq__ from typed fields: @dataclass class JobConfig: source: str; retries: int = 3. Better than dicts for configs/records — typo-safe attribute access, defaults, type hints, and IDE support — with less boilerplate than manual classes.

questions.q: What is duck typing? How does it differ from interfaces/ABCs?
questions.a: Duck typing: an object's suitability comes from the methods it implements, not its declared type — 'if it quacks'. ABCs/protocols formalize expected interfaces when you want isinstance checks or static verification without giving up flexibility.

questions.q: How do you read and write files efficiently in Python (streaming large files line by line, csv module, json module)?
questions.a: Stream instead of slurping: iterate file objects line-by-line, use csv.reader/DictReader for delimited data, json.load for whole documents vs json.loads per line for JSONL. Always pass encoding explicitly and use newline='' with csv writers.

questions.q: How do you handle dates and times robustly (datetime, timezone-aware vs naive, ISO 8601 parsing)?
questions.a: Use datetime with explicit tzinfo (zoneinfo); store/compare in UTC, convert at edges. Parse ISO 8601 with datetime.fromisoformat (or dateutil for messy formats). Naive-vs-aware mixing raises errors or, worse, silently wrong offsets — normalize on ingestion.

questions.q: What are f-strings and common string operations you use daily in data work?
questions.a: F-strings interpolate expressions with formatting: f"{amount:,.2f}", f"{dt:%Y-%m-%d}". Daily staples: .strip(), .split(), .join(), .lower(), .replace(), .startswith(), and re for pattern extraction.

questions.q: How does sorting work — sorted vs .sort, key functions, sorting by multiple fields, stability?
questions.a: sorted returns a new list; .sort() mutates in place. key= computes the sort basis: sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (r['region'], -r['sales'])) for multi-field ordering. Python's sort is stable — equal keys keep original order, enabling multi-pass sorts.

questions.q: What do zip, enumerate, any, all, and itertools utilities do? Give data-processing examples.
questions.a: zip pairs iterables element-wise; enumerate yields (index, item); any/all short-circuit boolean checks across iterables; itertools provides chain (concatenate), groupby (consecutive grouping), islice (lazy slicing), product/combinations — building blocks for memory-light record processing.

questions.q: How do you connect to databases from Python (DB-API, SQLAlchemy, connection pooling, parameterized queries)?
questions.a: Use SQLAlchemy (or DB-API drivers like pyodbc) with engine/connection pooling; always parameterize queries (execute(text(sql), params)) — never f-string values into SQL. Use context managers for connections/transactions and pd.read_sql for analysis pulls.

questions.q: How do you call REST APIs in Python (requests, pagination, retries with backoff, rate limits, auth)?
questions.a: requests with a Session for pooling; handle pagination via next-page tokens/links in a loop; implement retries with exponential backoff (urllib3 Retry or custom) honoring Retry-After on 429s; authenticate via headers/OAuth; always set timeouts and raise_for_status().

questions.q: How do you structure a Python ETL project (config, logging, src layout, entry points) for maintainability?
questions.a: Layout: src/package modules (extract/transform/load separated), config/ per environment, tests/, entry-point CLI, pyproject.toml for dependencies. Keep pure transformation functions separate from I/O so logic is unit-testable; configuration injected, not hardcoded.

questions.q: How do you implement logging properly (logging module vs print, levels, handlers, structured logs)?
questions.a: Use the logging module with module-level loggers (logging.getLogger(__name__)), levels (DEBUG→CRITICAL), and handlers/formatters set once at entry point. Structured logs (JSON with run_id, row counts) make pipeline runs queryable; print offers none of this and can't be filtered or routed.

questions.q: How do you write unit tests with pytest (fixtures, parametrize, mocking external systems)?
questions.a: pytest discovers test_*.py functions with plain asserts; fixtures provide reusable setup (sample frames, temp dirs, fake configs); @pytest.mark.parametrize runs one test across many cases; monkeypatch/unittest.mock replace APIs, clocks, and databases so tests are fast and deterministic.

questions.q: What is the difference between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests for a data pipeline?
questions.a: Unit tests verify pure functions on tiny in-memory data (fast, run every commit); integration tests exercise real components — a test database, real files, Spark local (slower, run in CI); end-to-end tests run the whole pipeline on sample data in a staging environment validating outputs and orchestration.

questions.q: How do you profile slow Python code (timeit, cProfile, memory_profiler) and what are common speedups?
questions.a: Profile before optimizing: timeit for micro-benchmarks, cProfile+snakeviz for hotspots, memory_profiler/tracemalloc for allocation. Common wins: replace row loops with vectorized pandas/NumPy, use sets/dicts for lookups, batch I/O and DB round-trips, and cache repeated computations.

questions.q: Why are vectorized operations (NumPy/pandas) faster than Python loops?
questions.a: Vectorized operations execute in compiled C over contiguous arrays with SIMD and no per-element interpreter overhead or boxing — typically 10–100x faster than Python-level loops doing the same arithmetic element by element.

questions.q: What are common gotchas with floating point arithmetic in financial/metric calculations, and when do you use Decimal?
questions.a: Binary floats can't represent many decimals exactly (0.1+0.2 != 0.3), so equality checks and cumulative sums drift. Use math.isclose for comparisons, round only at presentation, and use Decimal (or integer minor units) for money and anywhere ledger-exact arithmetic is required.

questions.q: How do you parse and validate JSON safely, including nested/optional fields?
questions.a: json.loads inside try/except for malformed payloads; access nested optional fields with .get chains or a small helper; validate structure with pydantic models when shape matters — turning missing/renamed fields into explicit validation errors instead of KeyErrors mid-pipeline.

questions.q: How do you handle secrets and credentials in Python code (env vars, key vaults — never hardcoding)?
questions.a: Read from environment variables or a secrets manager (Key Vault) at runtime; never commit secrets or hardcode them. Use .env only locally (gitignored), rotate credentials, and prefer managed identities over static secrets where the platform allows.

questions.q: What is pickling/serialization and when is it unsafe?
questions.a: Pickle serializes arbitrary Python objects — convenient for caches, but unpickling executes code, so never unpickle untrusted data. Prefer JSON/Parquet for data interchange; pickle only for trusted internal artifacts within one controlled environment and Python version.

questions.q: Explain error handling and idempotency when writing a script that loads data daily — how do you make reruns safe?
questions.a: Make reruns safe by keying work to the load window: delete-then-insert (or MERGE) for the target partition, write to staging then atomically swap, record processed batch IDs to skip duplicates, and make side effects (notifications) conditional on first success.

questions.q: How do you schedule/parametrize a Python script for different environments (argparse/click, config files, env-based settings)?
questions.a: Use argparse/click for CLI parameters (dates, environment, dry-run flags); load environment-specific settings from config files or env vars merged with defaults; keep one codebase where environment is data, not branched code — the orchestrator passes parameters per run.

questions.q: What are walrus operator, unpacking, and other modern syntax features you actually use?
questions.a: The walrus operator assigns within expressions (while (chunk := f.read(65536)):); unpacking spreads sequences (a, *rest = xs; merged = {**d1, **d2}); pathlib for filesystem paths; match statements for structured dispatch — modern syntax that tightens data-handling code.

questions.q: What is the difference between @staticmethod, @classmethod, and instance methods?
questions.a: Instance methods receive self and act on object state; @classmethod receives cls — alternate constructors like from_config(); @staticmethod receives neither — namespaced utility functions logically belonging to the class.

questions.q: How would you process a 50 GB CSV on a machine with 8 GB RAM using only Python?
questions.a: Stream it: iterate with csv.reader aggregating incrementally, or pandas read_csv(chunksize=...) combining per-chunk aggregates, or better, use DuckDB/Polars lazy scan which process larger-than-memory CSVs with predicate pushdown. Never load the whole file; select only needed columns.

questions.q: How do you detect and handle bad records (schema drift, encoding issues, malformed rows) in file ingestion?
questions.a: Validate early: explicit dtypes/schema on read, try/except around parsing with bad rows routed to a quarantine file with reasons, encoding detection/explicit encoding, row-length checks, and counts of rejected rows logged and alerted — so drift is visible, not silent.

questions.q: Write the logic (pseudo or real) for a function that retries an API call with exponential backoff and jitter.
questions.a: import random, time; def call_with_retry(fn, max_tries=5, base=1.0): for i in range(max_tries): try: return fn() except RetryableError: if i == max_tries-1: raise; sleep = base * (2**i) + random.uniform(0, base); time.sleep(sleep). Jitter prevents synchronized retry storms; only retry retryable errors.

questions.q: Describe a Python automation you built that saved real time — what design decisions made it reliable?
questions.a: Strong answers name reliability decisions, not just the task: idempotent reruns, config-driven parameters, structured logging with row counts, validation gates before writes, alerts on failure, and documentation — e.g., an automated reconciliation script that replaced a manual Excel process with logged, rerunnable checks.

questions.q: What is a DataFrame and a Series? How does the index work and why is it central to pandas?
questions.a: A DataFrame is a 2D table of columns (each a Series) sharing a row index; a Series is one labeled 1D array. The index labels rows and drives alignment: arithmetic and joins match on index labels, not position — the source of both power and silent bugs.

questions.q: How do loc, iloc, and at/iat differ? Give examples of label vs positional selection.
questions.a: loc selects by labels (df.loc['2025-01', ['sales']], inclusive slices); iloc by integer position (df.iloc[0:5, 1:3], exclusive end); at/iat are fast scalar accessors for single cells. Mixing them up on integer-labeled indexes is a classic error.

questions.q: What is boolean masking/filtering and how do you combine multiple conditions correctly (&, |, parentheses)?
questions.a: A boolean mask is a True/False Series used to filter: df[(df.amount > 0) & (df.region == 'GCC')]. Use & | ~ (not and/or) and parenthesize every condition because comparison operators bind looser than &.

questions.q: What is the SettingWithCopyWarning, what causes it, and how does copy-on-write (pandas 2.x) change things?
questions.a: It warns that you may be modifying a temporary copy via chained indexing (df[mask]['col'] = x), leaving the original unchanged. Fix with df.loc[mask, 'col'] = x. Pandas 2.x copy-on-write makes chained assignment consistently not modify the original, removing the ambiguity.

questions.q: How do you read data efficiently (read_csv options: dtype, usecols, parse_dates, chunksize, nrows)?
questions.a: Pass dtype= to avoid inference cost and wrong types, usecols= to read only needed columns, parse_dates= for datetimes, chunksize= to stream large files, nrows= for quick inspection. Explicit dtypes on IDs prevent leading-zero loss and float-ification of nullable ints.

questions.q: What are pandas dtypes, and why do object columns hurt memory and speed? What is the category dtype?
questions.a: Dtypes determine storage and speed: int64/float64/datetime64 are fast NumPy arrays; object columns hold Python objects (usually strings) — slow and memory-hungry. category maps repeated strings to integer codes — huge savings for low-cardinality columns like country or status.

questions.q: How do nullable dtypes (Int64, boolean, string) differ from NumPy dtypes, and how does NaN vs None vs pd.NA behave?
questions.a: Nullable dtypes (Int64, boolean, string) support pd.NA without upcasting to float — classic pandas turns an int column with a missing value into float64 with NaN. NaN is a float, None is a Python object, pd.NA is the unified missing marker; behavior differs in comparisons and groupby.

questions.q: How do you profile and reduce a DataFrame's memory usage?
