questions.a: df.info(memory_usage='deep') and df.memory_usage(deep=True) reveal true footprint. Reduce by downcasting numerics (int32/float32), converting strings to category, parsing dates properly, dropping unused columns at read time, and using Arrow-backed dtypes.

questions.q: How do you handle missing data: isna, fillna, dropna, interpolate — and how do you decide which is analytically correct?
questions.a: isna flags missing; dropna removes; fillna imputes (constant, ffill for carrying forward observations); interpolate estimates between points for ordered series. The analytical decision matters most: filling revenue with 0 vs excluding it changes conclusions — choose per column meaning.

questions.q: How do you find and remove duplicates (duplicated, drop_duplicates, keep parameter)?
questions.a: duplicated() flags repeat rows (subset= for key columns, keep= controls which occurrence survives); drop_duplicates removes them. For 'latest record per key', sort by timestamp then drop_duplicates(subset=key, keep='last') — deliberate keep choice is the difference between right and wrong data.

questions.q: Explain merge vs join vs concat. Map SQL joins to pandas merge how= options.
questions.a: merge is SQL-style joining on columns (how='inner/left/right/outer/cross'); join is index-based merge sugar; concat stacks DataFrames vertically (axis=0, like UNION ALL) or horizontally. SQL INNER/LEFT/FULL map directly to merge how= values.

questions.q: What do the validate and indicator arguments in merge do, and why should you use them?
questions.a: validate='one_to_many' etc. asserts key uniqueness expectations and raises on violation — catching fan-out at the join instead of in wrong totals later. indicator=True adds a _merge column (left_only/right_only/both) for reconciliation analysis.

questions.q: How does groupby work (split-apply-combine)? Difference between agg, transform, apply, and filter on groups?
questions.a: groupby splits rows by key, applies a function per group, and combines results. agg computes aggregates (collapses to one row per group); transform returns a result aligned to the original rows (group share, group mean for imputation); apply runs arbitrary functions (flexible, slowest); filter keeps/drops whole groups.

questions.q: How do you compute multiple named aggregations per group in one pass?
questions.a: Named aggregation: df.groupby('region').agg(total=('amount','sum'), orders=('order_id','nunique'), avg_val=('amount','mean')) — one pass, clean output column names.

questions.q: When is groupby().apply() a performance trap and what are alternatives?
questions.a: apply calls a Python function per group with overhead per call — thousands of groups make it crawl. Alternatives: built-in agg/transform (vectorized per group), vectorizing the logic before grouping, or engine alternatives (numba, Polars, DuckDB) for complex per-group logic.

questions.q: What are pivot, pivot_table, melt, stack, and unstack? When do you reshape wide↔long?
questions.a: pivot reshapes long→wide (fails on duplicate index/column pairs); pivot_table aggregates duplicates (aggfunc); melt goes wide→long (tidy data for modeling/plotting); stack/unstack pivot index levels. Reshape long for analysis pipelines, wide for human-readable reports.

questions.q: What is a MultiIndex? How do you select from it, and when is reset_index the right move?
questions.a: A MultiIndex has multiple levels of row/column labels — typically from groupby on several keys. Select with .loc[('A', 2025)], xs(), or IndexSlice. reset_index() is right whenever you're about to merge, export, or the hierarchy adds friction rather than meaning.

questions.q: How do window operations work: rolling, expanding, ewm? Compute a 7-day moving average per group.
questions.a: rolling computes fixed-window stats, expanding computes cumulative from start, ewm weights recent values more. Per group: df.groupby('store')['sales'].transform(lambda s: s.rolling(7, min_periods=1).mean()) — or sort and use groupby().rolling() with droplevel.

questions.q: How do shift and diff work? Compute month-over-month change per customer.
questions.a: shift moves values down/up within order (previous row); diff is value minus shifted value. MoM per customer: df.sort_values(['cust','month']).groupby('cust')['amount'].diff() — or pct_change() for percentage.

questions.q: How do rank and qcut/cut differ for ranking and bucketing?
questions.a: rank() assigns numeric ranks with tie methods (average/min/dense); cut bins values into fixed intervals you define (business thresholds); qcut bins by quantiles for equal-sized buckets (quartiles, deciles) — cut for meaning, qcut for distribution.

questions.q: How do you work with datetime columns (to_datetime, dt accessor, resample for time-series aggregation)?
questions.a: Convert with pd.to_datetime (specify format for speed/safety); access parts via .dt (year, month, day_name); resample('MS').sum() aggregates a datetime index to monthly. Datetime as real dtype unlocks time slicing (df.loc['2025-06']) and joins on dates.

questions.q: What is the difference between resample and groupby(pd.Grouper(...))?
questions.a: resample works on a datetime index/column for frequency conversion with time-aware semantics; groupby(pd.Grouper(key='dt', freq='MS')) does the same inside a groupby, letting you combine time bucketing with other keys (region + month).

questions.q: How do you handle time zones in pandas?
questions.a: tz_localize attaches a timezone to naive timestamps; tz_convert translates between zones. Store UTC, convert for display; comparing naive and aware timestamps raises — normalize at ingestion, and mind DST when localizing ambiguous local times.

questions.q: How do you do string operations at scale (str accessor, extract with regex, contains, split/explode)?
questions.a: The .str accessor vectorizes string ops: .str.strip/lower/replace/contains/extract(regex with groups)/split(expand=True). Regex-powered .str.extract turns messy codes into clean columns; case=False and na= parameters handle real-world mess.

questions.q: What does explode do and when do you need it (lists/JSON in cells)?
questions.a: explode expands list-like cells into one row per element, repeating other columns — essential after splitting delimited strings or normalizing JSON arrays (order → one row per item). Follow with type fixes since exploded values are often objects.

questions.q: How do you flatten nested JSON into a DataFrame (json_normalize)?
questions.a: pd.json_normalize flattens nested dicts into columns (sep='_' paths) and, with record_path/meta, expands nested arrays into rows while carrying parent fields — the standard API-response-to-DataFrame tool.

questions.q: What are vectorized operations vs apply vs itertuples vs iterrows — rank them by performance and explain why.
questions.a: Fastest to slowest: vectorized column operations (C speed) > .map on a Series > itertuples (namedtuples, no per-row Series construction) > apply(axis=1) > iterrows (builds a Series per row, dtype-mangling). If you're writing iterrows, look for the vectorized formulation first.

questions.q: What do map, replace, and np.where/np.select do for conditional column creation?
questions.a: map applies a dict/function to a Series (value translation); replace substitutes values possibly with regex; np.where(cond, a, b) is a vectorized if/else; np.select([conds], [choices], default) handles multi-branch logic — all vastly faster than row-wise apply.

questions.q: What is method chaining with assign and pipe, and why does it improve readability and reduce bugs?
questions.a: Chaining pipes each step's output forward: (df.query('amount>0').assign(margin=lambda d: d.rev-d.cost).groupby('region').agg(...)). assign adds columns without mutation; pipe inserts custom functions. Benefits: no intermediate-variable state bugs, readable top-to-bottom recipes.

questions.q: How do you rename, reorder, and change dtypes of columns cleanly?
questions.a: rename(columns={...}) or set df.columns from a cleaned list; reorder by indexing df[cols]; convert with astype({'id':'int64'}) or targeted converters (to_datetime, to_numeric with errors='coerce'). Do all typing once, early, in a dedicated cleaning step.

questions.q: How do you compare two DataFrames for equality or reconcile differences (compare, merge with indicator)?
questions.a: df.compare(other) shows aligned cell differences; for keyed reconciliation, merge on keys with indicator=True and suffixes, then filter mismatched rows/columns; assert_frame_equal for exact test equality. Always align dtypes and sort before comparing.

questions.q: How do you sample data (sample, head/tail by group)?
questions.a: sample(n= or frac=, random_state= for reproducibility) for random samples; stratified sampling via groupby().sample(); head/tail per group via groupby().head(n) which keeps the first n rows of each group without collapsing.

questions.q: How do you get top-N rows per group?
questions.a: Top-N per group: df.sort_values(['grp','metric'], ascending=[True,False]).groupby('grp').head(3) — or nlargest via group apply for a single metric. The sort+head pattern is fastest and clearest.

questions.q: What are common causes of silent wrong answers in pandas (index misalignment, join duplication, NaN in group keys)?
questions.a: Silent-wrong-answer causes: join key duplication inflating sums, index misalignment during assignment (values matched by label, not position), NaN group keys silently dropped by groupby (dropna=True default), lossy dtype coercions, and chained assignment not sticking. Defenses: validate= on merges, asserts on row counts and key uniqueness.

questions.q: How does index alignment affect arithmetic between Series/DataFrames?
questions.a: Operations between Series/DataFrames align on index labels first, filling non-matches with NaN — adding two Series with different indexes yields NaN where labels don't intersect. reset or explicitly align (reindex) when position-based math is intended, or use .values deliberately.

questions.q: How do you write data out (to_parquet, to_csv, to_sql) and why is Parquet preferred for analytics?
questions.a: to_parquet preserves dtypes, compresses well, and reads back fast with column selection — the default for pipeline interchange. to_csv is for human/legacy consumption (lossy types); to_sql loads to databases (use chunksize and fast drivers). Parquet's columnar layout matches analytics access patterns.

questions.q: What is Apache Arrow and how does the pandas Arrow backend change dtypes and performance?
questions.a: Arrow is a standardized in-memory columnar format. With dtype_backend='pyarrow', pandas gets proper string/nullable types, lower memory, faster I/O, and zero-copy interchange with Polars/DuckDB/Spark — increasingly the performance-default backend.

questions.q: When does pandas stop being the right tool? Compare with Polars, DuckDB, Dask, and Spark — and how you'd choose.
questions.a: Pandas suits datasets fitting comfortably in memory with single-machine workflows. Polars: faster multi-threaded engine with lazy optimization, similar scale ceiling. DuckDB: SQL over larger-than-memory files, excellent for joins/aggregation. Dask: parallel/out-of-core pandas API. Spark: cluster-scale and production distributed pipelines. Choose the lightest tool that fits data size and team skills.

questions.q: How do you process a file larger than memory in pandas (chunksize pattern) and aggregate across chunks?
questions.a: Loop over read_csv(chunksize=1_000_000), compute per-chunk partial aggregates (sums, counts, per-key dicts), combine at the end (sum of sums; weighted means from sums/counts). Works for distributive aggregations; for joins/medians at that scale, use DuckDB instead.

questions.q: How do you implement an SCD-style comparison (detect new/changed/deleted rows between snapshots) in pandas?
questions.a: Full-outer merge current vs previous snapshot on business keys with indicator: right_only=new, left_only=deleted, both=compare attribute hashes (or column-wise equality) to flag changed. Output insert/update/delete sets — the same logic that feeds an SCD process.

questions.q: How do you validate a DataFrame's schema and quality programmatically (assertions, pandera/Great Expectations)?
questions.a: Programmatic validation: assert on shape, dtypes, key uniqueness (df.key.is_unique), null thresholds, and value ranges after each transformation; pandera schemas or Great Expectations suites formalize these checks as declarative, reusable, CI-runnable contracts.

questions.q: How do you handle categorical encoding for reporting vs ML (astype('category'), get_dummies)?
questions.a: For reporting: astype('category') to fix sort orders (ordered categories) and save memory. For ML: pd.get_dummies for one-hot encoding (drop_first to avoid collinearity), or leave encoding to sklearn transformers within a pipeline for train/serve consistency.

questions.q: What is the pitfall of chained indexing (df[a][b]) and the correct alternative?
questions.a: df['a']['b'] performs two separate indexing operations — reading may work, but assigning through it modifies an intermediate that may be a copy. Always use single-step df.loc[rows, cols] for both reading and assignment.

questions.q: How do crosstab and pivot_table with margins support quick analysis?
questions.a: pd.crosstab counts (or aggregates) combinations of two-plus categoricals with normalize= for percentages; pivot_table(margins=True) adds row/column totals. Both are quick contingency/summary views before formal modeling.

questions.q: How do you compute percentage of total within groups (transform pattern)?
questions.a: Percent of group total: df['pct'] = df.amount / df.groupby('region').amount.transform('sum'). transform broadcasts the group aggregate back to every row, avoiding a merge.

questions.q: How do you merge on nearest keys or time (merge_asof) — e.g., matching trades to quotes?
questions.a: merge_asof joins each left row to the nearest earlier (or nearest, with direction=) right row on a sorted key — matching trades to latest quote, events to most recent config version. Both sides must be sorted; by= adds exact-match grouping keys.

questions.q: How do you deal with mixed encodings and messy real-world CSVs?
questions.a: Try utf-8 first, fall back per-file (encoding='cp1252'/'latin-1'), or detect with charset-normalizer; read with on_bad_lines to route or skip malformed rows, engine='python' for irregular delimiters, and normalize unicode/whitespace after load. Log every fallback so upstream fixes happen.

questions.q: How do you unit test pandas transformation functions (small fixture frames, assert_frame_equal)?
questions.a: Structure transformations as pure functions (frame in, frame out), feed small hand-built fixture frames covering normal + edge cases (nulls, duplicates, empty), assert with pd.testing.assert_frame_equal (check_dtype as appropriate) and targeted asserts on keys and aggregates.

questions.q: Describe a full EDA workflow you follow on a new dataset before building anything.
questions.a: EDA sequence: shape/dtypes/info; head/tail/sample sanity; missingness profile per column; descriptive stats and distributions for numerics; cardinality/top values for categoricals; key uniqueness and duplicates; time coverage and gaps; relationships between key fields; document anomalies and decisions before transforming anything.

questions.q: You receive a daily 5M-row transactions file and must produce clean monthly KPIs. Design the pandas pipeline: cleaning, typing, dedup, joins, aggregation, and output format.
questions.a: Pipeline: read with explicit dtypes and parse_dates; validate schema and row counts vs control totals; standardize strings/currencies; quarantine bad rows with reasons; dedupe on business key keeping latest; join reference dimensions with validate='many_to_one'; derive month and KPIs via groupby agg; assert totals reconcile to input; write monthly Parquet partitions plus a load-audit log row.

questions.q: What is Microsoft Fabric and how does it unify Data Factory, Synapse-style engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics, and Power BI?
questions.a: Fabric is Microsoft's unified SaaS analytics platform: Data Factory (integration), Data Engineering (Spark), Data Warehouse, Real-Time Intelligence, Data Science, and Power BI share one storage layer (OneLake), one capacity model, one governance/security surface — replacing stitched-together PaaS services.

questions.q: What is OneLake? Explain the 'one copy' philosophy and how it compares to a traditional data lake setup.
questions.a: OneLake is the single, tenant-wide logical data lake (built on ADLS Gen2) that all Fabric workloads read/write. 'One copy' means engines (Spark, SQL, Power BI Direct Lake, KQL) operate on the same Delta Parquet files instead of each maintaining its own copy — shortcuts extend this virtually to external storage.

questions.q: What is a Fabric capacity (F SKUs)? How do capacity units, smoothing, bursting, and throttling work?
questions.a: A capacity (F2–F2048) is purchased compute powering all Fabric workloads, measured in capacity units. Smoothing spreads usage over time windows; bursting borrows beyond baseline temporarily; sustained overload triggers throttling — interactive delays first, then rejections — so sizing and workload isolation matter.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Lakehouse and a Warehouse in Fabric, and how do you choose between them?
questions.a: A Lakehouse is files + Delta tables managed via Spark, flexible for engineering and semi-structured data, with a read-only SQL endpoint. A Warehouse is a full T-SQL engine with multi-table transactions, T-SQL DML/DDL. Choose Lakehouse for Spark-first teams and raw/varied data; Warehouse for SQL-first teams needing T-SQL writes.

questions.q: What is the SQL analytics endpoint of a Lakehouse and what are its limitations (read-only, sync latency)?
questions.a: It exposes Lakehouse Delta tables to T-SQL clients (and Power BI) automatically. Limitations: read-only (no INSERT/UPDATE), Delta-only visibility, and metadata sync latency after Spark writes — a known cause of 'stale data' confusion downstream.

questions.q: Explain Delta Lake as Fabric's storage format — why is everything Delta Parquet underneath?
questions.a: Every Fabric table is Delta Lake: Parquet data files plus a JSON transaction log providing ACID transactions, time travel, schema enforcement, and concurrent reader/writer safety. Standardizing on Delta is what lets all engines share one copy.

questions.q: What are OneLake shortcuts and how do they enable data virtualization across workspaces, ADLS, and even S3?
questions.a: Shortcuts are pointers in OneLake to data elsewhere — other workspaces, ADLS Gen2, Amazon S3, Dataverse — appearing as local folders/tables without copying. They enable cross-domain sharing and gradual migrations, with access governed at the shortcut target.

questions.q: What is mirroring in Fabric and when would you mirror a database instead of building ETL?
questions.a: Mirroring continuously replicates operational databases (Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, Snowflake) into OneLake as Delta with near-real-time CDC — zero-ETL analytics on operational data. Use it when you need current source data queryable without building ingestion pipelines.

questions.q: Explain Direct Lake mode: how it works, when it falls back to DirectQuery, and how framing/reframing affects it.
questions.a: Direct Lake loads Delta Parquet column data straight into memory on demand — Import-like speed with no scheduled copy. Framing pins the model to a table version; refresh is just re-framing (metadata). It falls back to DirectQuery for unsupported features (certain views, security setups, guardrail limits) — silently costing performance.

questions.q: Compare Import vs DirectQuery vs Direct Lake for a Fabric semantic model — decision criteria?
questions.a: Import: best raw performance and full features, needs refresh cycles and duplicates data. DirectQuery: real-time, source-bound performance limits. Direct Lake: near-Import speed on lakehouse data with no data duplication — the Fabric default when data is already Delta and features are compatible; verify fallback behavior.

questions.q: What are the main compute experiences in Fabric (Data Engineering notebooks, Data Factory pipelines, Dataflows Gen2, Warehouse SQL, Real-Time Intelligence)?
questions.a: Data Engineering: Spark notebooks and lakehouses for code-first transformation. Data Factory: pipelines (orchestration/copy) and Dataflows Gen2 (low-code Power Query). Warehouse: T-SQL analytics. Real-Time Intelligence: Eventstreams and KQL for streaming. Plus Power BI for semantic models/reports — all on OneLake.

questions.q: What is a Fabric notebook and how does the Spark runtime work (starter pools, custom pools, high concurrency mode)?
questions.a: Fabric notebooks run Spark (PySpark/Scala/SparkSQL/R) with lakehouses attached. Starter pools give fast session start with default sizing; custom pools tune node size/autoscale; high-concurrency mode shares one Spark session across notebooks/users for cost and startup efficiency.

questions.q: What is the difference between Dataflows Gen2 and pipelines? When do you use each — or both together?
questions.a: Dataflows Gen2 is low-code Power Query with data destinations — analyst-friendly transformation. Pipelines orchestrate: copy activities, control flow, scheduling, calling notebooks and dataflows. Typical pattern: pipeline orchestrates ingestion, then triggers dataflows or notebooks for transformation.

questions.q: How do pipelines in Fabric compare to Azure Data Factory? What activities do you commonly use (Copy, Notebook, dataflow, Invoke)?
questions.a: Fabric pipelines are ADF's successor inside Fabric: same concepts (Copy activity, ForEach, Lookup, If, parameters), tighter OneLake integration, some connector/IR differences (on-prem access via gateway rather than self-hosted IR). Common activities: Copy, Notebook, Dataflow, Stored procedure, Web/Invoke.

questions.q: How do you implement medallion architecture (Bronze/Silver/Gold) in Fabric? Which engine handles each layer in your design?
questions.a: Bronze lands raw immutable data (files/Delta, append-only); Silver cleans, dedupes, conforms types and keys (Spark notebooks typically); Gold serves dimensional/star models for the semantic layer (notebooks or Warehouse SQL). Each layer is separate lakehouse/schema with clear contracts; Direct Lake models sit on Gold.

questions.q: How do you ingest data incrementally in Fabric (watermarks, CDC, incremental copy patterns)?
questions.a: Incremental patterns: watermark columns tracked in a control table (pipeline Lookup → filtered Copy), Delta MERGE in notebooks for upserts, mirroring/CDC for databases, and incremental refresh for Dataflows Gen2. Log high-water marks after each successful load for restartability.

questions.q: What is the Copy activity vs COPY INTO vs notebook-based ingestion — trade-offs?
questions.a: Copy activity: configuration-driven bulk movement, best connector breadth. COPY INTO: T-SQL bulk load into Warehouse from files. Notebook ingestion: full control, validation, complex sources/APIs — more code to own. Start with Copy for movement; notebooks when logic exceeds configuration.

questions.q: How do you parameterize pipelines and notebooks for reusable, environment-aware pipelines?
questions.a: Parameterize pipelines (parameters + expressions on connections/paths) and notebooks (parameter cells receiving pipeline values) so one artifact serves all environments and sources — the foundation of metadata-driven frameworks and clean deployment across Dev/Test/Prod.

questions.q: How do you orchestrate dependencies and scheduling in Fabric (pipeline triggers, notebook scheduling, orchestration patterns)?
questions.a: Schedule pipelines (or event triggers), chain activities with dependencies, call notebooks/dataflows inline; notebook-only jobs can be scheduled directly. Complex dependency graphs use a master pipeline invoking child pipelines; monitor centrally via Monitoring hub.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Fabric Warehouse and Azure Synapse Dedicated SQL Pool?
questions.a: Fabric Warehouse is SaaS: automatic scaling within capacity, storage as open Delta in OneLake, no distribution-key management; Synapse dedicated pools are provisioned DWUs with hash-distribution design and proprietary storage. Fabric trades knob control for simplicity and open format.

questions.q: What T-SQL surface differences/limitations exist in Fabric Warehouse compared to SQL Server?
questions.a: Differences from SQL Server: historically limited constraint enforcement (PK/unique not enforced), some T-SQL surface gaps (certain identity/merge behaviors evolving), case-sensitive default collation considerations, no cross-database three-part queries outside the workspace model. Check current docs — the gap narrows continuously.

questions.q: How do V-Order and optimized write improve Delta performance in Fabric?
questions.a: V-Order is Microsoft's write-time Parquet optimization (sorting, encoding, compression tuning) making files dramatically faster for VertiPaq/Direct Lake reads; optimized write targets healthy file sizes instead of many small files. Both are on by default in most Fabric write paths.

questions.q: How do you run OPTIMIZE and VACUUM in Fabric, and why does small-file compaction matter?
questions.a: OPTIMIZE compacts small files (optionally V-Order) via table maintenance or Spark SQL; VACUUM removes unreferenced files past retention (mind time-travel needs). Streaming/frequent small writes demand scheduled compaction — small files degrade every downstream reader including Direct Lake.

questions.q: What is the semantic model's role in Fabric and how do you build one on top of a Lakehouse for Power BI?
questions.a: The semantic model is the metric/relationship layer over Gold tables that Power BI queries. Build via Direct Lake on the lakehouse: define relationships, DAX measures, RLS; keep one certified model per domain serving many reports — the contract between engineering and the business.

questions.q: How does workspace design work in Fabric — how would you structure workspaces across domains, environments, and layers?
questions.a: Common pattern: workspaces per layer×environment (e.g., Sales-Dev/Test/Prod) or per domain with medallion inside; separate engineering workspaces from consumer-facing report workspaces; capacity assignment per workload criticality. Fewer, well-governed workspaces beat sprawl.

questions.q: What are domains in Fabric and how do they support data mesh-style organization?
questions.a: Domains group workspaces by business area with delegated domain admins and branding — supporting data-mesh operating models: domain ownership of data products, federated governance from the center, easier discovery in the OneLake catalog.

questions.q: How does Git integration work in Fabric (connect workspace to Azure DevOps/GitHub, commit, branch out)?
questions.a: Connect a workspace to an Azure DevOps/GitHub branch; supported items (notebooks, semantic models, reports, pipelines) serialize to source files; commit/update from the workspace; developers branch out to isolated workspaces, PR back, and sync main to upstream environments.

questions.q: What are deployment pipelines in Fabric and how do deployment rules handle environment-specific connections?
questions.a: Deployment pipelines promote items Dev→Test→Prod between workspaces with diff views; deployment rules rebind environment-specific settings (lakehouse connections, parameters) per stage. Combine Git (versioning/PR) with deployment pipelines (promotion) or drive everything via fabric-cicd/APIs from DevOps.

questions.q: How do you implement security in Fabric: workspace roles, item permissions, OneLake data access roles, and sharing?
questions.a: Layers: workspace roles (Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer) for content management; item-level sharing for granular access; OneLake data access roles for folder/table-level lakehouse security; SQL permissions in Warehouse; plus semantic-model RLS for report consumers. Grant least privilege at the narrowest effective layer.

questions.q: How does RLS/OLS in semantic models interact with Direct Lake and Lakehouse security?
questions.a: Semantic-model RLS/OLS applies to users on the model; but Direct Lake queries read the lakehouse — under fixed identity, model RLS governs; if falling back or users hit the SQL endpoint directly, lakehouse/SQL security applies. Align both layers so bypass paths don't leak data.

questions.q: What is Microsoft Purview integration in Fabric — sensitivity labels, endorsement, lineage?
questions.a: Purview integration provides sensitivity labels flowing from source through reports, endorsement (promoted/certified), lineage views across items, and estate-wide scanning/glossary via the Purview hub — governance evidence for audits and trust signals for consumers.

questions.q: How do you monitor Fabric: Monitoring hub, capacity metrics app, Spark monitoring, pipeline run history?
questions.a: Monitoring hub shows run history/status for pipelines, notebooks, refreshes; the Capacity Metrics app breaks down CU consumption by item/operation for throttling analysis; Spark monitoring exposes job/executor detail; alerting via Data Activator or pipeline failure activities to Teams/email.

questions.q: What causes capacity throttling and how do you investigate and remediate interactive vs background operation overload?
questions.a: Throttling arises when sustained CU demand exceeds capacity after smoothing — symptoms: slow interactive queries, delayed/rejected jobs. Investigate with the metrics app to find top-consuming items/operations; remediate by optimizing offenders, rescheduling background load, isolating workloads across capacities, or scaling the SKU.

questions.q: What is Real-Time Intelligence (Eventstream, Eventhouse/KQL database) and give a use case.
questions.a: Real-Time Intelligence ingests streams via Eventstream (Event Hubs, IoT, CDC sources) into Eventhouse/KQL databases for sub-second analytics. Use case: live shipment-tracking telemetry powering operational dashboards and threshold alerts alongside batch analytics.

questions.q: What is KQL and how does it differ from SQL at a high level?
questions.a: KQL (Kusto) is a pipe-based query language optimized for logs/telemetry/time-series: table | where ts > ago(1h) | summarize count() by bin(ts, 5m). It excels at time-window aggregation and text/trace exploration; SQL remains the relational workhorse.

questions.q: What is Data Activator (Reflex/alerts) and how do you trigger actions from data conditions?
questions.a: Data Activator (Reflex) monitors data streams/query results for conditions (threshold breached, value changed, pattern over time) and triggers actions — Teams/email alerts, Power Automate flows, pipeline runs — no-code operational alerting on your data.

questions.q: How do you use Fabric's SQL database (transactional) offering and when would it fit?
questions.a: Fabric SQL database is an OLTP-capable SQL database within Fabric whose data auto-replicates to OneLake for analytics — fitting operational apps that want built-in analytical availability without separate ETL.

questions.q: How do notebooks read/write across Lakehouses and Warehouses (mounts, ABFS paths, spark connectors, T-SQL magic)?
questions.a: Notebooks attach lakehouses (default lakehouse for relative paths), read via spark.read.table or abfss:// paths, write Delta with saveAsTable; cross-workspace access via shortcuts or full ABFS paths; Warehouse tables reachable through the SQL endpoint connector or T-SQL magic; %%sql magic runs SparkSQL inline.

questions.q: What is semantic link (sempy) and how can notebooks read from semantic models?
questions.a: Semantic link (sempy) lets notebooks read semantic models — evaluate DAX, pull measures/tables into pandas/Spark, run model quality checks programmatically — bridging data science and the BI layer (e.g., validating measures against Silver data automatically).

questions.q: How do you handle schema evolution in Fabric Lakehouse tables?
questions.a: Delta supports additive evolution with mergeSchema on write and column mapping for renames/drops; overwriteSchema replaces schemas deliberately. Govern changes: additive by default, versioned contracts for breaking changes, and communicate to semantic-model owners since Direct Lake sees schema immediately.

questions.q: What are materialized lake views / metadata-driven pipelines patterns you'd use for scale?
questions.a: Materialized lake views (declarative, auto-refreshed Silver/Gold transformations) reduce hand-built orchestration; metadata-driven frameworks store source/table configs in control tables and loop them with parameterized pipelines/notebooks — onboarding source #50 becomes a config row, not new code.

questions.q: How do you migrate an existing Synapse or ADF + ADLS + Power BI stack to Fabric — what's your assessment approach?
questions.a: Assess inventory (ADF pipelines, Synapse pools, ADLS layout, Power BI models), map to Fabric equivalents (pipelines, notebooks/Warehouse, OneLake shortcuts to existing ADLS for zero-copy migration start), migrate incrementally domain-by-domain with parallel-run validation, and convert Import models to Direct Lake where guardrails allow.

questions.q: How does licensing work for consumers of Fabric content (F64 threshold for free viewers, Pro requirements)?
questions.a: Content in F64+ capacity workspaces is viewable by users with Free licenses (viewer role); below F64, consumers need Pro. Authors/publishers need Pro regardless. This threshold often drives capacity sizing economics for large report audiences.

questions.q: How do you estimate and control costs in Fabric (capacity sizing, pausing, workload distribution)?
questions.a: Estimate from workload simulation on trial capacity using the metrics app; control costs by right-sizing SKU, pausing dev capacities off-hours (PAYG), scheduling background jobs off-peak, optimizing hot items, and splitting capacities to isolate expensive workloads from interactive BI.

questions.q: What is the difference between staging and non-staged Dataflow Gen2 writes, and the performance implications?
questions.a: Staged Gen2 writes land data in an internal staging lakehouse before the destination, enabling engine-assisted (fast copy/SQL) processing of large volumes; non-staged writes go direct — simpler for small loads. Large merges benefit from staging; misconfigured staging is a common Gen2 performance complaint.

questions.q: How do you implement data quality checks in a Fabric pipeline (notebook asserts, pipeline fail activities, logging tables)?
questions.a: Implement quality gates as notebook assertions (row counts, null/key checks) that raise to fail the pipeline activity, DQ result tables logged per run, pipeline If/fail activities acting on check outputs, and alerts on failure — quarantine bad batches in Bronze rather than letting them poison Silver.

questions.q: How do you implement CI/CD for Fabric items end-to-end (Git branches, PRs, deployment pipelines, fabric-cicd/APIs)?
questions.a: End-to-end CI/CD: feature workspaces from Git branches → PR with review into main → workspace sync (or fabric-cicd/Fabric APIs in Azure DevOps pipelines) deploying to Dev → deployment pipeline or scripted promotion to Test/Prod with deployment rules rebinding connections → automated post-deploy validation notebooks.

questions.q: How do you test a Direct Lake model's performance and diagnose fallback to DirectQuery?
questions.a: Test with Performance Analyzer and DAX Studio timings against realistic concurrency; check DirectLakeBehavior/fallback via analysis tools (queries hitting DirectQuery instead of memory), guardrail limits (row counts per SKU), framing recency, and file health (V-Order, compaction) — most 'slow Direct Lake' is fallback or small files.

questions.q: Describe an end-to-end Fabric solution you would design: sources → ingestion → Bronze/Silver/Gold → semantic model → report → monitoring — with reasoning for each choice.
questions.a: Design: sources land via mirroring/pipelines/API notebooks into Bronze lakehouse; Spark notebooks conform to Silver (dedupe, SCD, quality gates); Gold star schema built via notebooks or Warehouse; certified Direct Lake semantic model with RLS; Power BI app for consumers; orchestrated by parameterized pipelines; monitored via Monitoring hub + capacity metrics; Git + deployment pipelines for lifecycle.

questions.q: A Direct Lake report shows stale data after a pipeline run. Walk through the possible causes (framing, refresh, SQL endpoint sync) and fixes.
questions.a: Stale Direct Lake data causes: model not re-framed after load (refresh the model — cheap metadata operation), SQL analytics endpoint metadata sync lag, pipeline wrote to a different lakehouse/table than modeled, fallback querying a stale cache path, or automatic framing disabled. Verify Delta commit timestamps, sync the endpoint, then re-frame and retest.

questions.q: What is Apache Spark and how does it differ from MapReduce? Why is in-memory processing faster?
questions.a: Spark is a distributed compute engine processing data across a cluster in memory. MapReduce writes intermediate results to disk between every map/reduce stage; Spark keeps data in memory across a DAG of operations and only shuffles when required — orders of magnitude faster for iterative and multi-step jobs.

questions.q: Explain Spark's architecture: driver, executors, cluster manager, cores, and how a job is distributed.
questions.a: The driver runs your program, builds the DAG, and schedules tasks; executors are JVM processes on workers running tasks and caching data; the cluster manager (YARN/Kubernetes/standalone/Databricks) allocates resources. Each executor has cores (task slots) and memory; a job is split into tasks distributed to slots.

questions.q: What are jobs, stages, and tasks? What causes a stage boundary?
questions.a: An action spawns a job; a job splits into stages at shuffle boundaries; each stage runs one task per partition. Wide dependencies (data must move between partitions) force a stage boundary — the shuffle write/read separating stages.

questions.q: What is a shuffle, why is it expensive, and which operations trigger it?
questions.a: A shuffle redistributes data across the cluster by key: map tasks write sorted/partitioned files, reduce tasks fetch their partitions over the network. It's expensive because of disk I/O, serialization, and network transfer. Triggered by joins (non-broadcast), groupBy/agg, distinct, repartition, and orderBy.

questions.q: Explain transformations vs actions and lazy evaluation. Why does laziness matter?
questions.a: Transformations (select, filter, join) build a lazy logical plan; actions (count, collect, write) trigger execution. Laziness lets Catalyst optimize the entire plan — pushing filters early, pruning columns — instead of executing operations naively in written order.

questions.q: What is the difference between narrow and wide transformations?
questions.a: Narrow transformations need only one parent partition per output partition (map, filter) — pipelined within a stage. Wide transformations need data from many partitions (groupByKey, join, distinct) — requiring a shuffle and new stage.

questions.q: What are RDDs, DataFrames, and Datasets? Why are DataFrames preferred today?
questions.a: RDDs are the low-level distributed object collections (no schema, no optimization). DataFrames add schema and run through Catalyst/Tungsten — optimized columnar execution. Datasets add compile-time typing (Scala/Java only). Use DataFrames; drop to RDDs only for exotic low-level needs.

questions.q: What is the Catalyst optimizer and what optimizations does it perform (predicate pushdown, column pruning, constant folding)?
questions.a: Catalyst converts your query through logical/physical plans applying rule-based and cost-based optimization: predicate pushdown (filters to the source/scan), column pruning (read only needed columns), constant folding, join reordering, and choosing physical join strategies.

questions.q: What is the Tungsten engine / whole-stage codegen?
questions.a: Tungsten is the execution layer: off-heap binary memory format avoiding JVM object overhead, cache-friendly processing, and whole-stage code generation — compiling operator chains into single JVM functions eliminating virtual call overhead per row.

questions.q: What is Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) and what does it fix at runtime (skew joins, coalescing partitions, join strategy switch)?
questions.a: AQE re-optimizes at runtime using real shuffle statistics: coalesces many small post-shuffle partitions, switches sort-merge joins to broadcast when a side turns out small, and splits skewed partitions into subtasks. It fixes plans that static estimates got wrong — leave it on.

questions.q: Explain partitions in Spark. How do you choose the number of shuffle partitions?
questions.a: A partition is the unit of parallelism — one task processes one partition. Shuffle partitions default to 200 (spark.sql.shuffle.partitions); tune so partitions are roughly 100–200 MB, or rely on AQE coalescing. Too few = underutilization and memory pressure; too many = scheduling overhead and small files.

questions.q: What is the difference between repartition and coalesce?
questions.a: repartition(n or cols) fully reshuffles to n partitions or by column hash — even distribution, full shuffle cost, usable to increase partitions. coalesce(n) merges existing partitions without shuffle — cheap for reducing partition count (pre-write), but can create uneven sizes and can't increase count.

questions.q: What is data skew, how do you detect it in the Spark UI, and how do you fix it (salting, AQE, broadcast)?
questions.a: Skew: a few keys hold most data, so their tasks run far longer — visible in the Spark UI as stages where max task duration/input dwarfs the median. Fixes: AQE skew-join handling, salting hot keys (append random suffix, replicate the other side), broadcasting the smaller table, or isolating hot keys into a separate handled path.

questions.q: What is a broadcast join and when does Spark choose it? How do you force or block it?
questions.a: A broadcast join ships the small table to every executor, joining without shuffling the large side. Spark auto-broadcasts under spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (default 10 MB); force with broadcast(df) hint; block by setting threshold -1. Beware broadcasting tables too big for driver/executor memory.

questions.q: Compare join strategies: broadcast hash, shuffle hash, sort-merge. When does each win?
questions.a: Broadcast hash: one side small — no shuffle, fastest. Shuffle hash: both shuffled, smaller side hashed in memory — good when one side is much smaller but too big to broadcast. Sort-merge: both shuffled and sorted — the scalable default for two large tables. AQE can demote/promote between them at runtime.

questions.q: What is caching/persisting? Explain storage levels and when caching helps vs hurts.
questions.a: cache()/persist() store a DataFrame's computed partitions (MEMORY_AND_DISK default) for reuse across multiple actions — valuable for iterative access to the same intermediate. Costs memory that competes with execution; caching something used once is pure overhead. Unpersist when done.

questions.q: What is checkpointing and how does it differ from caching?
questions.a: Checkpointing writes data to reliable storage and truncates lineage — useful for very long lineage chains (iterative algorithms, streaming state) where recomputation or stack depth becomes a problem. Cache is temporary and lineage-preserving; checkpoint is durable and lineage-cutting.

questions.q: How does Spark achieve fault tolerance (lineage, DAG recomputation)?
questions.a: Each partition's lineage (the chain of transformations from source) is recorded; on executor loss, missing partitions are recomputed from lineage on other nodes. Shuffle files and caching reduce recomputation scope; checkpoints cut lineage for long chains.

questions.q: Explain spark-submit and key configs: executor memory, executor cores, driver memory, dynamic allocation.
questions.a: spark-submit deploys jobs with resource configs: --executor-memory, --executor-cores, --num-executors (or dynamic allocation min/max), --driver-memory. Balanced sizing: ~4–5 cores per executor, memory per core matched to data; dynamic allocation scales executors with load on shared clusters.

questions.q: How does Spark memory management work (unified memory, execution vs storage, off-heap)? What causes OOM in executors vs driver?
questions.a: Unified memory splits executor heap into execution (shuffles, joins, sorts) and storage (cache) regions that borrow from each other. Executor OOM: oversized partitions, skew, huge broadcasts, memory-hungry UDFs. Driver OOM: collect() on big data, too many tasks/partitions metadata, large broadcast creation.

questions.q: What does collect() do and why is it dangerous? What are safer alternatives?
questions.a: collect() ships the entire distributed dataset to the driver — OOM risk and cluster-to-single-machine bottleneck. Alternatives: show()/limit() for inspection, take(n) for samples, write() for outputs, toPandas() only on aggregated/small results.

questions.q: What are UDFs in PySpark, why are they slow, and how do pandas (vectorized) UDFs improve them? Why prefer built-in functions?
questions.a: Python UDFs serialize rows to a Python worker per executor, breaking codegen and columnar flow — slow. Pandas UDFs batch via Arrow into vectorized pandas operations — much faster. Built-in functions (pyspark.sql.functions) run in the JVM with full optimization — always prefer them; UDFs are the last resort.

questions.q: How do you read/write data in PySpark (formats, options, modes: overwrite/append/errorifexists/ignore)?
questions.a: spark.read.format('parquet'/'csv'/'json'/'delta').options(...).load(path); write with df.write.format(...).mode(m).save(path). Modes: overwrite replaces, append adds, errorifexists (default) fails on existing, ignore skips silently. Prefer explicit schemas over inference in production.

questions.q: Why is Parquet the default analytics format? Explain row groups, encoding, and predicate pushdown.
questions.a: Parquet is columnar with per-column encoding/compression: readers scan only referenced columns (column pruning), row-group min/max statistics enable predicate pushdown skipping chunks, and splittable files parallelize well — ideal for analytical scan-heavy access.

questions.q: How do you handle schemas: inferSchema vs explicit StructType, and schema evolution options (mergeSchema)?
questions.a: inferSchema samples data (extra pass, wrong guesses on messy data); explicit StructType is deterministic and fast — mandatory for production CSV/JSON. Delta enforces schema on write; mergeSchema opts into additive evolution; overwriteSchema replaces intentionally.

questions.q: How do you handle corrupt records when reading files (PERMISSIVE, DROPMALFORMED, FAILFAST, _corrupt_record)?
questions.a: CSV/JSON readers offer modes: PERMISSIVE (default) nulls bad fields and captures raw text into _corrupt_record for quarantine analysis; DROPMALFORMED discards bad rows; FAILFAST errors immediately. Production pattern: PERMISSIVE + route corrupt records to a rejects table with counts alerted.

questions.q: Explain the withColumn, select, filter/where, groupBy/agg API — and why chaining many withColumns can be slow.
questions.a: withColumn adds/replaces one column; select projects/computes many at once; filter/where filters rows; groupBy().agg() aggregates. Long withColumn chains bloat the logical plan (analysis overhead) — prefer a single select with multiple expressions, or selectExpr, for many derivations.

questions.q: How do window functions work in PySpark (Window.partitionBy/orderBy, rowsBetween)? Give a dedup-latest-record example.
questions.a: Window: from pyspark.sql.window import Window; w = Window.partitionBy('key').orderBy(F.col('updated').desc()); df.withColumn('rn', F.row_number().over(w)).filter('rn=1') — the latest-record-per-key dedup. rowsBetween defines frames for running/rolling aggregates.

questions.q: How do you dedupe data at scale: dropDuplicates vs window row_number — trade-offs?
questions.a: dropDuplicates(keys) keeps an arbitrary row per key — fine when duplicates are identical. The window row_number pattern picks a deterministic winner (latest timestamp) — required when duplicates differ. Both shuffle; window adds a sort but gives control.

questions.q: How do explode, arrays, maps, and structs work? How do you flatten deeply nested JSON in PySpark?
questions.a: Arrays/maps/structs model nested data; explode flattens arrays to rows (explode_outer keeps empties); dot notation and getField access struct members; flatten deeply nested JSON iteratively: explode arrays, select struct fields to top level, repeat — or use higher-order functions (transform, filter) to process arrays without exploding.

questions.q: What is the difference between Spark SQL and the DataFrame API — do they perform differently?
questions.a: They compile to the same plans through Catalyst — performance is equivalent. Spark SQL suits SQL-fluent teams and set-based logic; the DataFrame API composes programmatically (loops, conditionals, testing). Mix freely: createOrReplaceTempView bridges them.

questions.q: How do temp views, global temp views, and catalog tables (managed vs external) differ?
questions.a: Temp views are session-scoped names over DataFrames; global temp views live in global_temp across sessions on one application; catalog tables persist in the metastore — managed tables let Spark own data lifecycle (drop deletes data), external tables reference paths (drop keeps data).

questions.q: How do you optimize small files problems on write (repartition before write, maxRecordsPerFile, compaction)?
questions.a: Small files: repartition/coalesce to target ~128 MB–1 GB files before write, set maxRecordsPerFile, enable optimized write (Delta/Databricks), and run OPTIMIZE compaction on Delta tables regularly — small files inflate metadata, task counts, and read latency platform-wide.

questions.q: What is partitionBy on write (hive-style partitioning) and how do you choose partition columns? What is partition pruning?
questions.a: partitionBy('date') writes hive-style directory partitions; queries filtering the partition column read only matching directories (partition pruning). Choose low-cardinality, commonly-filtered columns (date, region). Over-partitioning (high-cardinality keys) creates a small-files catastrophe.

questions.q: What is bucketing and when does it help joins?
questions.a: Bucketing pre-hashes data into fixed buckets by key at write; joins/aggregations on the bucket key can avoid shuffling when bucket specs match. Useful for repeated large joins on the same key; less used in Delta world where liquid clustering/Z-order and AQE cover most needs.

questions.q: What is Delta Lake? Explain the transaction log, ACID guarantees, and time travel.
questions.a: Delta Lake adds a transaction log (_delta_log JSON/checkpoints) over Parquet: ACID commits, concurrent reader/writer isolation via optimistic concurrency, schema enforcement/evolution, time travel to prior versions, and DML (UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE) — turning a lake into a lakehouse.

questions.q: How does MERGE INTO work in Delta, and how do you implement upserts and SCD2 with it?
questions.a: MERGE INTO target USING source ON keys WHEN MATCHED [AND cond] THEN UPDATE SET ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT ... — atomic upserts. SCD2: match on business key + current flag; when matched and hash changed, update to close the old row and insert the new version (two-pass or union trick for insert-on-change).

questions.q: What are OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER (or liquid clustering), and VACUUM in Delta?
questions.a: OPTIMIZE compacts small files into large ones; Z-ORDER co-locates data by high-selectivity filter columns for data skipping (liquid clustering is its successor — incremental, no full rewrite, evolvable keys); VACUUM deletes files unreferenced beyond retention (default 7 days) — balancing storage vs time travel.

questions.q: How do you implement incremental processing (watermark columns, Delta Change Data Feed, Structured Streaming)?
questions.a: Incremental options: watermark column filters (process rows newer than last high-water mark stored in a control table), Delta Change Data Feed (read row-level changes between versions), and Structured Streaming with Delta sources (checkpoint-tracked exactly-once incremental consumption) — trigger.availableNow for batch-style runs.

questions.q: Explain Structured Streaming basics: micro-batches, triggers, checkpoints, output modes, exactly-once semantics.
questions.a: Structured Streaming processes micro-batches from sources (files, Kafka, Delta) with a checkpoint directory storing progress/state — enabling exactly-once with idempotent/transactional sinks. Triggers control cadence (processingTime, availableNow); output modes: append (new rows), update (changed aggregates), complete (full result).

questions.q: What are watermarks in streaming and how do they handle late data?
questions.a: Watermarks bound event-time lateness for stateful operations: withWatermark('event_time', '1 hour') admits data up to 1 hour late, finalizing windows and evicting state beyond it. Later data is dropped — the trade between completeness and unbounded state growth.

questions.q: How do you monitor and debug a Spark job in the Spark UI (stages, tasks, spill, GC time, skewed task duration)?
questions.a: Spark UI: Jobs/Stages show duration, task distribution (min/median/max — skew detection), shuffle read/write sizes, and spills; Executors show GC time and memory; SQL tab shows the physical plan with per-operator metrics. Start from the longest stage, inspect its slowest tasks, and read the plan feeding it.

questions.q: What is a spill to disk and what config/code changes reduce it?
questions.a: Spill occurs when execution memory can't hold a shuffle/sort/join working set, writing to disk (visible in stage metrics as memory/disk spill). Reduce with more partitions (smaller per-task data), more executor memory or fewer concurrent cores, AQE, salting skew, and avoiding wide rows through early projection.

questions.q: How do you tune a chronically slow Spark job — walk through your systematic checklist.
questions.a: Systematic tuning: read the Spark UI (longest stage, skew, spills, GC); check plan for unexpected scans/joins order/missing pushdown; right-size shuffle partitions or trust AQE; broadcast appropriately; eliminate UDFs; cache reused intermediates; fix small files at sources; scale/rebalance cluster only after the plan is sane.

questions.q: What is the difference between client and cluster deploy modes?
questions.a: Client mode runs the driver on your submitting machine (notebooks, dev) — driver dies if your session dies; cluster mode runs the driver on the cluster (production jobs) — resilient and closer to executors.

questions.q: How does PySpark actually execute Python code (JVM, Py4J, serialization overhead) and what is Arrow's role?
questions.a: The PySpark driver builds JVM plans via Py4J; execution happens in the JVM. Only Python UDFs invoke Python workers per executor with serialization overhead; Arrow accelerates JVM↔Python transfers (pandas UDFs, toPandas). Hence: DataFrame API = JVM speed; row-wise Python = pay the bridge toll.

questions.q: How do you test PySpark code (local SparkSession, chispa/assertDataFrameEqual, fixture data)?
questions.a: Test with a local SparkSession fixture (pytest, session-scoped), tiny hand-built DataFrames, pure transformation functions (df in → df out), and assertions via chispa or pyspark.testing.assertDataFrameEqual; keep I/O at the edges so logic tests need no cluster or real storage.

questions.q: What is the cost of count(), distinct(), and orderBy() on large data — and cheaper alternatives for each intent?
questions.a: count() scans everything (fine, but don't call repeatedly — cache first if reused); distinct() is a full shuffle — prefer approx_count_distinct for cardinality estimates; orderBy() globally sorts (range partition + sort) — use sortWithinPartitions or top-N via window/limit patterns when global order isn't truly needed.

questions.q: Design a PySpark job that ingests daily JSON files, validates, dedupes, and merges into a partitioned Delta table idempotently.
questions.a: Design: explicit schema read of the day's files (badRecordsPath/PERMISSIVE quarantine); validate counts and required fields against thresholds; dedupe via row_number over business key ordered by event time; MERGE into the Delta target on business key (idempotent — reruns re-merge the same day harmlessly); partition by event date; log metrics and OPTIMIZE on schedule.

questions.q: Your join of two large tables runs for hours and one task runs forever. Diagnose and fix — cover skew detection, salting, broadcast thresholds, and AQE.
questions.a: Diagnose: Spark UI stage metrics — if one task's input/duration dwarfs peers, it's skew; find the hot key via groupBy count on join keys. Fix: enable AQE skew handling; broadcast the smaller side if it fits (raise threshold deliberately); salt the hot keys (explode small side across salt range); or split hot keys into a separate broadcast-joined path and union results.

questions.q: What is Databricks and how does the lakehouse platform differ from a warehouse-plus-lake architecture?
questions.a: Databricks is a managed lakehouse platform unifying data engineering, SQL analytics, and ML on open formats (Delta/Parquet) with collaborative notebooks, jobs, and governance (Unity Catalog). Versus warehouse-plus-lake: one copy of data, one security model, and both SQL and Spark/ML engines over the same tables.

questions.q: Explain the Databricks architecture: control plane vs compute (data) plane. What stays in your cloud account?
questions.a: The control plane (Databricks account: UI, job scheduler, notebook code, metadata) runs in Databricks' cloud; the compute/data plane (clusters, your data in ADLS/S3) runs in your cloud subscription — data stays in your tenancy; serverless shifts compute into Databricks-managed accounts with isolation guarantees.

questions.q: What cluster types exist (all-purpose, job clusters, SQL warehouses, serverless) and when do you use each?
questions.a: All-purpose clusters: interactive development, shared, expensive to leave running. Job clusters: created per job run, cheaper DBUs, isolated, terminate on completion — the production default. SQL warehouses: Photon-powered SQL endpoints for BI/analysts (serverless option). Serverless compute: instant-start managed capacity for jobs/notebooks/DLT.

questions.q: How do you size and configure a cluster (node types, autoscaling, spot instances, Photon)?
questions.a: Choose node types by workload (memory-optimized for joins/wide aggregations, compute-optimized for CPU-heavy parsing); enable autoscaling with sensible min/max; spot instances for fault-tolerant batch at steep discount (with on-demand driver); Photon for SQL/DataFrame-heavy pipelines; auto-termination always for interactive.

questions.q: What is Photon and what workloads does it accelerate?
questions.a: Photon is Databricks' C++ vectorized execution engine, transparently accelerating SQL and DataFrame operations (scans, joins, aggregations, Delta writes) typically 2–5x — priced at a DBU premium that usually nets positive for SQL-style workloads; it doesn't accelerate Python UDFs.

questions.q: What are Databricks Runtime versions and why does pinning them matter?
questions.a: Runtimes bundle Spark, Delta, and library versions (plus ML variants). Pinning a runtime per job guarantees reproducible behavior; upgrades happen deliberately with testing, since Spark/Delta behavior changes across versions — 'it broke after the runtime auto-updated' is a preventable incident.

questions.q: What is Unity Catalog? Explain the three-level namespace (catalog.schema.table) and what problems it solves.
questions.a: Unity Catalog is the centralized governance layer: one metastore per region governing catalogs → schemas → tables/views/volumes/models across workspaces, with ANSI GRANTs, lineage capture, auditing, and cross-workspace sharing — replacing per-workspace Hive metastores and mount-point security.

questions.q: How does Unity Catalog handle permissions (GRANT model), lineage, and audit?
questions.a: Permissions are ANSI SQL GRANTs (USE CATALOG/SCHEMA, SELECT, MODIFY, CREATE, EXECUTE) on securables, inherited down the hierarchy, assigned to groups; lineage is captured automatically at table and column level from queries; audit logs record access — governance evidence and impact analysis built in.

questions.q: What are managed vs external tables in Unity Catalog, and where does the data live?
questions.a: Managed tables: UC controls both metadata and the data location (managed storage) — dropping deletes data; supports optimizations like predictive maintenance. External tables: data at your specified path, registered in UC — dropping removes only metadata. Prefer managed for full lifecycle governance; external for shared/legacy paths.

questions.q: What are volumes in Unity Catalog and how do they replace DBFS mounts for files?
questions.a: Volumes are UC-governed storage for non-tabular files (raw landing files, configs, model artifacts) with path access (/Volumes/catalog/schema/vol/...) — replacing DBFS mounts so file access follows the same GRANT model and audit as tables.

questions.q: What is Delta Sharing and when would you use it?
questions.a: Delta Sharing is an open protocol for sharing live Delta tables with external consumers (any platform, no Databricks required) or across metastores — no data copies, recipient reads current data with revocable grants. Use for partner data products and cross-org distribution.

questions.q: How do notebooks work in Databricks (magic commands, widgets for parameters, %run vs importing modules)?
questions.a: Notebooks support multiple languages via %python/%sql/%scala magics, widgets for parameters, %run to inline another notebook, and Repos-backed files so shared logic lives in .py modules imported normally — preferred over %run chains for testable code.

questions.q: What is Databricks Repos/Git folders and how do you structure notebook + module code for version control?
questions.a: Git folders (Repos) clone repositories into the workspace: develop on branches, commit/push from the UI or CLI, and structure projects as notebooks for orchestration entry points plus python packages for logic — enabling PR review and CI over Databricks code.

questions.q: How do you pass parameters into and results out of notebook jobs (widgets, dbutils.jobs.taskValues, job parameters)?
questions.a: Parameters: job parameters/widgets (dbutils.widgets.get) feed values in; dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set/get passes small values between tasks in a job; dbutils.notebook.exit returns a value to a caller. Keep payloads small — pass references (paths, dates), not data.

questions.q: What is dbutils and what are its common uses (fs, secrets, widgets)?
questions.a: dbutils provides workspace utilities: dbutils.fs (list/copy/rm files), dbutils.secrets.get (secret retrieval without exposure), dbutils.widgets (parameters), dbutils.jobs.taskValues (inter-task values) — the glue for operational notebook code.

questions.q: How do secrets and secret scopes work, including Azure Key Vault-backed scopes?
questions.a: Secret scopes store credentials accessed via dbutils.secrets.get(scope, key) with values redacted in output. Azure Key Vault-backed scopes read directly from AKV so rotation is centralized; access is governed by scope ACLs — never hardcode credentials in notebooks.

questions.q: What are Databricks Workflows (Jobs)? Explain tasks, dependencies, retries, schedules, and triggers (file arrival, continuous).
questions.a: Workflows define jobs as task DAGs (notebook, python wheel, SQL, dbt, DLT tasks) with depends_on, per-task clusters or shared job clusters, retries with backoff, schedules/cron, and triggers including file arrival and continuous mode; parameters flow to tasks; failure notifications built in.

questions.q: Job cluster vs all-purpose cluster for scheduled workloads — cost and isolation reasoning?
questions.a: Job clusters spin up per run: cheaper DBU rate, clean environment, isolation between runs, right-sized per job. All-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs waste money (idle time, dev contention) and risk dependency drift — use them only for interactive development.

questions.q: What is Delta Live Tables (DLT / Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines)? How do declarative pipelines differ from imperative notebooks?
questions.a: DLT (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) declares tables as queries with @dlt.table decorators; the framework infers the DAG, manages compute, handles retries, tracks quality metrics, and supports streaming and materialized tables. You state 'what', it manages 'how' — versus notebooks where you own orchestration and recovery.

questions.q: What are DLT expectations and how do they enforce data quality (warn, drop, fail)?
questions.a: Expectations are declarative row-level constraints on DLT tables: @dlt.expect (log violations), expect_or_drop (discard bad rows), expect_or_fail (abort). Violation metrics land in the pipeline event log — quality enforcement and observability without hand-rolled checks.

questions.q: What is Auto Loader (cloudFiles)? How does it track processed files and handle schema inference/evolution?
questions.a: Auto Loader (format 'cloudFiles') incrementally ingests new files from cloud storage using file notification or listing, tracking processed files in checkpoint state (exactly-once), inferring and evolving schema with rescue of unexpected columns (_rescued_data), scaling to millions of files — the standard landing-zone reader.

questions.q: Compare Auto Loader vs COPY INTO vs plain spark.read for ingestion.
questions.a: Auto Loader: continuous/incremental file discovery, schema evolution, scale — the default for ongoing ingestion. COPY INTO: idempotent SQL bulk load, good for periodic manual/simple loads. spark.read: one-off full reads with no processed-file tracking — you own incrementality.

questions.q: How do you implement medallion architecture in Databricks — concretely, what happens in Bronze, Silver, Gold?
questions.a: Bronze: raw append of source data (Auto Loader), minimal transformation, retains history. Silver: dedupe, type conformance, quality gates, business keys, joins into clean entity tables (MERGE/CDC application). Gold: dimensional models and aggregates serving BI/ML — each layer a schema/catalog with explicit contracts.

questions.q: How do you implement SCD Type 1 and Type 2 in Databricks (MERGE, DLT apply_changes)?
questions.a: SCD1: MERGE matching business key, update-in-place attributes. SCD2: MERGE closing changed current rows (end_date, is_current=false) and inserting new versions; or DLT's apply_changes/AUTO CDC with stored_as_scd_type=2 handling sequencing, out-of-order events, and history columns declaratively.

questions.q: What is Change Data Feed in Delta and how does it enable incremental downstream processing?
questions.a: CDF (delta.enableChangeDataFeed) records row-level inserts/updates/deletes with version metadata; downstream reads table_changes between versions to process only deltas — enabling incremental Silver→Gold without full recomputes and feeding external sync consumers.

questions.q: What is liquid clustering and how does it compare to partitioning + Z-ORDER?
questions.a: Liquid clustering replaces partitioning + Z-ORDER: cluster keys co-locate data incrementally without directory explosion, keys can change without rewrites, and it handles skewed/high-cardinality columns gracefully — the current recommendation for new large tables (CLUSTER BY).

questions.q: What are deletion vectors and predictive optimization?
questions.a: Deletion vectors mark rows deleted without rewriting files, making DELETE/UPDATE/MERGE far cheaper (reads apply vectors); predictive optimization lets Databricks automatically run OPTIMIZE/VACUUM/clustering maintenance on managed tables based on usage patterns — maintenance without cron jobs.

questions.q: How do you handle GDPR-style deletes in a Delta lakehouse (vacuum retention, CDF implications)?
questions.a: Right-to-be-forgotten: DELETE removes rows logically, but old files persist for time travel — run VACUUM past retention to physically purge, mind CDF retaining change rows, and document the purge SLA (e.g., deletes physical within 7+ days). Design PII into few tables to limit blast radius.

questions.q: What is Databricks SQL? How do SQL warehouses, queries, alerts, and dashboards fit analyst workflows?
questions.a: Databricks SQL provides SQL warehouses for BI-scale concurrency, a SQL editor, saved queries, alerts (threshold-triggered notifications), dashboards, and query history/profiles — making the lakehouse a warehouse-grade serving layer for analysts.

questions.q: How does Databricks connect to Power BI / other BI tools (Partner Connect, SQL warehouse endpoints, OAuth)?
questions.a: Power BI connects via the Databricks connector to a SQL warehouse (Import or DirectQuery), authenticating with Entra ID/OAuth (preferred over PATs); Partner Connect automates setup. Serverless warehouses minimize latency; Photon + result caching make DirectQuery viable for many models.

questions.q: What is the Databricks CLI / REST API / SDK and what have you automated with them?
questions.a: CLI/REST/SDKs automate everything: deploying jobs, managing clusters/permissions, triggering runs, exporting artifacts. Typical automation: CI pipelines validating and deploying bundles, operational scripts for user/grant management, run-triggering from external orchestrators.

questions.q: What are Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs) and how do they enable CI/CD for jobs and pipelines?
questions.a: Asset Bundles (DABs) define jobs, pipelines, and code as YAML + source in Git, with environment targets (dev/staging/prod variable substitution); databricks bundle deploy/run applies them — infrastructure-as-code for Databricks enabling reviewable, repeatable deployments.

questions.q: How do you design CI/CD for Databricks with Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions (branching, testing, deploy to envs)?
questions.a: CI/CD: feature branches with unit tests on pure functions (local Spark) → PR validation pipeline (lint, tests, bundle validate) → merge deploys bundle to staging with integration test job on sample data → approval gate → prod bundle deploy; secrets from Key Vault; job configs versioned, never hand-edited in prod.

questions.q: How do you test Databricks code — unit testing modules outside notebooks, integration testing with sample data?
questions.a: Structure code as Python packages (wheel) with pure transformation functions unit-tested via local SparkSession in CI; notebooks only as thin entry points; integration tests run as staging jobs against fixture data in a test catalog asserting outputs, counts, and expectations.

questions.q: How do you monitor jobs and clusters (job run history, cluster metrics, system tables, alerting on failures)?
questions.a: Monitor via job run history and failure notifications (email/Teams/webhooks), cluster metrics UI, the Spark UI per run, and Unity Catalog system tables (billing, job run timelines, audit) queried for trends and SLA dashboards; alert on failures, duration anomalies, and cost spikes.

questions.q: What are system tables in Unity Catalog and how do you use them for cost and audit analysis?
questions.a: System tables (system.billing.usage, system.lakeflow/jobs run data, access audit) expose platform telemetry as queryable Delta tables — build cost-per-job dashboards, job SLA trend reports, audit investigations, and chargeback allocation directly in SQL.

questions.q: How do you control and reduce Databricks costs (cluster policies, auto-termination, spot, serverless, DBU analysis)?
questions.a: Cost levers: job clusters not all-purpose, auto-termination, right-sized autoscaling, spot workers, Photon where it nets positive, serverless for spiky workloads, cluster policies capping sizes, scheduling heavy work off-peak, monitoring DBU by job via system tables, and deleting zombie jobs/clusters.

questions.q: What are cluster policies and why do platform teams enforce them?
questions.a: Cluster policies are admin-defined templates constraining cluster creation (allowed node types, max workers, mandatory tags, auto-termination, spot settings) — enforcing cost control, tagging for chargeback, and configuration consistency while letting teams self-serve within guardrails.

questions.q: What are instance pools and when do they help?
questions.a: Instance pools hold pre-warmed idle VMs so clusters attach in seconds instead of minutes — valuable for many short job runs and latency-sensitive scheduled pipelines; idle pool capacity costs cloud VM price without DBUs, so size pools to demand patterns.

questions.q: How does Databricks integrate with ADLS Gen2 on Azure (service principals, managed identities, credential passthrough history → UC)?
questions.a: Access ADLS through Unity Catalog: storage credentials (managed identity of the access connector) + external locations govern paths centrally with GRANTs — replacing legacy per-cluster service principal configs, mount points, and credential passthrough; managed identities avoid secret rotation entirely.

questions.q: What is the difference between Databricks on Azure vs the same workloads in Microsoft Fabric — how would you position each?
questions.a: Databricks: code-first Spark platform, deepest engineering/streaming/ML capability, multicloud. Fabric: SaaS all-in-one tightly integrated with Power BI/Office, capacity-based pricing, faster for Microsoft-centric BI teams. They interoperate (Fabric can shortcut to ADLS Delta written by Databricks); position by team skills, workload complexity, and ecosystem gravity.

questions.q: What is MLflow and what do experiments, runs, and the model registry provide (even for a DE supporting DS teams)?
questions.a: MLflow tracks experiments (parameters, metrics, artifacts per run), packages models, and registers them in UC Model Registry with versions/aliases for controlled promotion — for a DE, it's the contract for handing reproducible features/models between DS and production serving.

questions.q: What is Feature Store at a high level?
questions.a: Feature Store centralizes feature definitions/tables so training and serving read identical features (with point-in-time correct joins), preventing training/serving skew and duplicate feature engineering across teams.

questions.q: How do you serve or expose Gold data to consumers (SQL warehouse, Delta Sharing, external tables, APIs)?
questions.a: Serving options: SQL warehouses for BI tools (Power BI DirectQuery/Import), Delta Sharing for external consumers, external tables read by other engines, feature/online tables and model serving for ML apps, or APIs over SQL execution endpoints — choose by consumer type and latency needs.

questions.q: How do you handle concurrent writes to the same Delta table (optimistic concurrency, conflict classes, retry patterns)?
questions.a: Delta uses optimistic concurrency: transactions validate at commit against the log; conflicting commits (overlapping files/partitions) raise ConcurrentModificationException classes. Mitigate by partition-disjoint writes, retry loops with backoff, avoiding concurrent OPTIMIZE with rewrites, and serializing writers per table where needed.

questions.q: How do you orchestrate Databricks from external tools (ADF/Airflow operators) and when do you prefer native Workflows?
questions.a: External orchestration (ADF's Databricks activities, Airflow's DatabricksSubmitRun/Jobs operators) suits estates with existing cross-system orchestrators — submit jobs via API and poll. Prefer native Workflows when the DAG is Databricks-internal: richer task types, repair runs, cheaper, less moving parts.

questions.q: What is table history/time travel used for operationally (debugging, rollback, reproducing runs)?
questions.a: Table history (DESCRIBE HISTORY) shows every commit with operation, user, and metrics — operationally used for debugging what changed and when, RESTORE to roll back bad loads, time-travel queries to reproduce reports as-of a version, and auditing write patterns.

questions.q: How do you implement an idempotent daily batch job in Databricks so reruns don't duplicate data?
questions.a: Idempotency: MERGE on business keys instead of blind appends; or overwrite the specific date partition (replaceWhere) per run; make file ingestion exactly-once via Auto Loader checkpoints; key notifications/side effects to run IDs; then any rerun converges to the same state.

questions.q: Describe your end-to-end design for migrating an on-prem SQL Server ETL to Databricks: landing, transformation, quality, orchestration, and BI serving.
questions.a: Migration design: land source extracts via ADF/Lakeflow connectors into Bronze (Auto Loader on files); rebuild transformations as PySpark/dbt on Databricks writing Silver/Gold Delta under Unity Catalog; enforce quality via expectations/tests; orchestrate with Workflows; parallel-run against the legacy ETL reconciling outputs; serve BI via SQL warehouse; cut over source-by-source with rollback via time travel.

questions.q: A nightly job's runtime doubled after a month in production. Walk through your investigation: data growth, small files, skew, cluster health, plan changes.
questions.a: Investigate in order: data volume growth (input metrics per run vs history); small-file accumulation (file counts, OPTIMIZE cadence); skew emergence (stage max vs median task time); plan changes (runtime upgrade, statistics, join strategy flips); cluster health (spot evictions, autoscale ceilings); and upstream latency (waiting on late files). System tables + run history give the trendline; fix the dominant factor, then re-baseline.

questions.q: What is dbt and what problem does it solve? Why 'ELT' with transformation in the warehouse?
questions.a: dbt is a transformation framework: SQL SELECT statements become version-controlled, tested, documented models that dbt compiles and runs in dependency order inside your warehouse. ELT loads raw data first, then transforms with the warehouse's own scalable compute — dbt brings software engineering discipline to that T.

questions.q: What is the difference between dbt Core and dbt Cloud?
questions.a: dbt Core is the open-source CLI you run/orchestrate yourself; dbt Cloud adds a managed scheduler, IDE, CI integration, hosted docs, and the semantic layer as a paid service. Core + Airflow/Workflows is a common self-managed equivalent.

questions.q: What is a dbt model? How does dbt compile SQL and decide execution order?
questions.a: A model is one SELECT statement in a .sql file; dbt wraps it in DDL per its materialization, compiles Jinja/refs to real names, and executes models in DAG order. One model = one table/view = one logical transformation step.

questions.q: Explain ref() and source() — why should you never hardcode table names?
