questions.a: ref('model') resolves to the correct database.schema.object per environment and registers the dependency edge in the DAG; source() does the same for declared raw tables. Hardcoding names breaks environment separation, lineage, and selective builds — the DAG only knows what ref/source tell it.

questions.q: What is the DAG in dbt and how does dependency inference actually work?
questions.a: The DAG is built entirely from ref()/source() calls parsed from model code — no manual ordering. dbt topologically sorts models, runs them in dependency order with configured threads parallelizing independent branches.

questions.q: What is a dbt project structure best practice (staging, intermediate, marts layers)?
questions.a: Standard structure: models/staging (one folder per source system; 1:1 with source tables; renaming, typing, light cleaning), models/intermediate (reusable business-logic joins), models/marts (facts and dimensions per domain). Staging views, marts tables/incremental — clear layers keep lineage legible.

questions.q: What naming conventions do you follow for staging vs mart models (stg_, int_, fct_, dim_)?
questions.a: Conventions: stg_<source>__<entity> for staging, int_<entity>_<verb> for intermediate, fct_<event> for facts and dim_<entity> for dimensions. Consistent prefixes make the DAG self-describing and enable selection by pattern.

questions.q: What are sources, and what do source freshness checks do?
questions.a: Sources declare raw tables in YAML (database/schema/table) with descriptions and tests, referenced via source(). Freshness checks (loaded_at_field with warn_after/error_after) verify raw data recency via dbt source freshness — catching upstream pipeline failures before transforming stale data.

questions.q: What are the model materializations: view, table, incremental, ephemeral — trade-offs of each?
questions.a: View: no storage, always current, compute at query time — staging default. Table: full rebuild each run — simple, fine for small/medium marts. Incremental: processes only new/changed data into an existing table — for large facts. Ephemeral: inlined as a CTE, no object — for lightweight shared logic (limits debuggability).

questions.q: How do incremental models work? Explain is_incremental(), the unique_key, and incremental strategies (append, merge, delete+insert, insert_overwrite).
questions.a: On incremental runs, dbt wraps your filter in is_incremental() (e.g., WHERE loaded_at > (SELECT MAX(loaded_at) FROM {{ this }})) and applies the configured strategy: append (insert only), merge (upsert on unique_key), delete+insert (replace matching keys), insert_overwrite (replace partitions). unique_key defines the merge grain.

questions.q: When does an incremental model need a --full-refresh, and what are the risks of late-arriving data?
questions.a: Full-refresh (--full-refresh rebuilds from scratch) is needed after logic changes affecting history, schema changes, or corruption. Risks: late-arriving data outside the incremental window is silently missed — mitigate with lookback windows (process last N days, merge dedupes) and periodic full refreshes.

questions.q: What are dbt snapshots and how do they implement SCD Type 2 (timestamp vs check strategy)?
questions.a: Snapshots capture SCD2 history of mutating sources: dbt compares current source rows to the snapshot table and versions changes with dbt_valid_from/to. Timestamp strategy trusts an updated_at column; check strategy compares configured columns — for sources without reliable timestamps.

questions.q: What are seeds and what are they appropriate for (and not)?
questions.a: Seeds are CSVs in the repo loaded via dbt seed — for small, static reference data (country codes, mappings) that belongs in version control. Not for real data loads: no scale, no lineage from sources, and PII in Git is a governance failure.

questions.q: Explain schema tests (generic tests): unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships. How do they run under the hood?
questions.a: Generic tests are YAML-declared assertions compiled to SQL returning failing rows: unique and not_null enforce grain/completeness, accepted_values enforces domains, relationships enforces referential integrity to another model. Any returned rows = test failure — data quality as code, run with every build.

questions.q: How do you write singular (bespoke) tests and custom generic tests?
questions.a: Singular tests are bespoke SQL files in tests/ returning rows that violate an expectation (e.g., revenue reconciliation between layers). Custom generic tests are parameterized test macros ({% test positive_value(model, column_name) %}) reusable in YAML across models.

questions.q: What are test severities (warn vs error) and store_failures — how do you operationalize test results?
questions.a: severity: warn logs without failing the build (new/noisy checks), error blocks (contract-critical checks); store_failures persists failing rows to audit tables for triage. Operationalize: alert on errors, review warn trends weekly, and promote stabilized warns to errors.

questions.q: What packages have you used (dbt_utils, dbt_expectations, codegen) and what do they add?
questions.a: dbt_utils: surrogate keys, date spines, union_relations, pivot, and extra generic tests. dbt_expectations: Great Expectations-style rich assertions (distributions, row counts vs source). codegen: generates staging model/YAML boilerplate from sources — accelerating standards-compliant scaffolding.

questions.q: What is Jinja in dbt? Give examples of loops/conditionals generating SQL.
questions.a: Jinja templates SQL before compilation: {% for status in ['open','closed'] %} sum(case when status='{{ status }}' then 1 end) as {{ status }}_count, {% endfor %} generates repetitive SQL; {% if target.name == 'prod' %} branches logic — metaprogramming that keeps SQL DRY.

questions.q: What are macros and how do you write and reuse one across models?
questions.a: Macros are reusable Jinja functions in macros/: {% macro cents_to_currency(col) %} round({{ col }}/100.0, 2) {% endmacro %}, called as {{ cents_to_currency('amount') }} in any model — centralizing business rules and warehouse-dialect quirks in one tested place.

questions.q: What are variables (var), environment variables, and how do you make models environment-aware?
questions.a: var('key', default) reads variables from dbt_project.yml or --vars CLI overrides (run dates, feature flags); env_var('NAME') reads environment variables (credentials, environment names). Combine with target properties to make models environment-aware without code changes.

questions.q: What is the target and profiles.yml? How do dev vs prod profiles/schemas work?
questions.a: The target is the active connection profile (warehouse, database, schema, threads) from profiles.yml; each developer targets a personal dev schema, CI targets a temp schema, prod targets production — same code, isolated outputs, selected by --target.

questions.q: How does dbt handle documentation (description fields, doc blocks, dbt docs generate, lineage graph)?
questions.a: YAML descriptions on models/columns plus {% docs %} markdown blocks compile via dbt docs generate into a browsable site with column-level docs, test coverage, and an interactive DAG lineage graph — documentation generated from the code that's actually running.

questions.q: What is the semantic layer / metrics concept in dbt at a high level?
questions.a: The semantic layer defines metrics (measures, dimensions, joins) once in dbt, served consistently to downstream tools via APIs — one governed definition of 'revenue' instead of each dashboard reinventing it. MetricFlow handles query generation.

questions.q: How do exposures declare downstream dependencies like Power BI dashboards?
questions.a: Exposures declare downstream consumers (dashboards, apps, ML jobs) in YAML with owner and dependencies — appearing in lineage so impact analysis covers 'which Power BI dashboards break if this model changes' and dbt can build/test everything an exposure needs.

questions.q: What are model contracts and constraints, and why do they matter for reliable interfaces?
questions.a: Contracts enforce a model's declared schema (column names, types, constraints) at build time — the model fails to build if it drifts from its contract. Essential for models consumed by other teams: interface stability becomes enforced, not hoped for.

questions.q: What are model versions and deprecations for breaking-change management?
questions.a: Model versions let you run v1 and v2 of a breaking-change model side by side with a deprecation window, while consumers migrate refs at their pace — managed breaking changes instead of coordinated big-bang cutovers.

questions.q: How do hooks work (pre-hook, post-hook, on-run-start/end)? Give practical uses (grants, audit logging).
questions.a: Hooks run SQL around model builds: pre-hook/post-hook per model (grants after build, audit-log inserts), on-run-start/on-run-end per invocation (create audit schemas, log run summaries). Grants are the canonical post-hook (or the grants config).

questions.q: What is state and deferral (--defer, state:modified) and how does 'slim CI' build only changed models?
questions.a: State comparison (--state path/to/prod/manifest) enables state:modified selection — build only models changed vs production and their children (slim CI); --defer resolves unbuilt upstream refs to production objects so CI needn't rebuild the whole DAG. PR pipelines become minutes, not hours.

questions.q: How do you structure a CI/CD pipeline for dbt (PR checks, test runs, prod deployment, artifacts)?
questions.a: CI/CD: PR triggers a job running dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer against a CI schema, plus SQLFluff linting; merge to main deploys and runs production build on schedule; artifacts (manifest) stored per environment for state comparison; failures block merge — transformations ship like software.

questions.q: How does dbt fit with Airflow or other orchestrators — how do you schedule and monitor dbt in production?
questions.a: Airflow (or Databricks Workflows/ADF) triggers dbt on schedule after upstream loads complete: BashOperator/dbt Cloud API/Cosmos rendering the dbt DAG as Airflow tasks. Orchestrator owns when and alerting; dbt owns transformation order within the run.

questions.q: What do run, test, build, compile, and ls commands each do — and why is 'dbt build' usually preferred?
questions.a: run executes models; test runs tests; build runs models, tests, snapshots, seeds interleaved in DAG order — a model's tests gate its downstream consumers, so build is the production default. compile renders SQL without executing; ls lists selected nodes for debugging selection.

questions.q: How do node selection syntax and graph operators work (model+, +model, tag:, path:)?
questions.a: Selection: dbt build --select my_model+ (model and descendants), +my_model (ancestors and model), tag:nightly, path:models/marts, intersections (tag:daily,marts) and exclusions (--exclude) — precise control over what builds when.

questions.q: What are tags and how do you use them for selective runs (e.g., nightly vs hourly)?
questions.a: Tags label models in config for operational grouping: tag daily vs hourly models, pii for governance, critical for priority alerting — then schedule dbt build --select tag:hourly independently of the nightly full build.

questions.q: How do you handle grain and uniqueness in fact models — how do tests encode the grain?
questions.a: Declare grain explicitly (one row per what?) and enforce it: unique test on the key (or dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns for composite grains), not_null on grain columns. Most downstream bugs are silent grain violations — tests make them loud at the source model.

questions.q: How do you implement a star schema in dbt — staging to dimensional marts workflow?
questions.a: Star schema workflow: staging models standardize each source; intermediate models resolve entity dedup and business logic; dim_ models build dimensions with surrogate keys (snapshots feeding SCD2 dims); fct_ models join facts to dimension keys at declared grain; tests enforce keys and relationships; exposures link the semantic model.

questions.q: How do you manage surrogate keys in dbt (dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key, hashing)?
questions.a: Use dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key([cols]) hashing business key columns into deterministic keys — stable across environments and rebuilds (unlike sequences), consistent for SCD2 versioning when combined with valid_from, and portable across warehouses.

questions.q: How does dbt work on different engines you know (Databricks, Fabric, SQL Server/Synapse) — adapters and dialect differences?
questions.a: Adapters translate dbt to each engine: dbt-databricks (Delta merges, catalogs), dbt-fabric/dbt-synapse (T-SQL dialect, different incremental strategies), dbt-sqlserver. Differences surface in supported incremental strategies, DDL quirks, and grants — macros with adapter dispatch handle cross-dialect logic.

questions.q: What does the dbt-databricks adapter offer (merge strategies, file formats, catalogs)?
questions.a: dbt-databricks supports Delta-native features: merge and insert_overwrite/replace_where incremental strategies, liquid clustering/partitioning configs, Unity Catalog three-level namespaces, SQL warehouse or cluster execution, and python models — making dbt a first-class lakehouse transformation layer.

questions.q: How do you optimize slow dbt models (materialization choice, incremental logic, warehouse-side tuning)?
questions.a: Optimize by materialization choice (incremental for big facts), tightening incremental predicates (partition pruning), pre-aggregating in intermediates rather than repeated joins, warehouse-side tuning (clustering, file compaction, warehouse sizing), and inspecting compiled SQL query plans exactly as you'd tune hand-written SQL.

questions.q: What are common anti-patterns in dbt projects (monolithic models, ref-less SQL, over-ephemeralization, untested marts)?
questions.a: Anti-patterns: 1,000-line monolith models (split into staging/intermediate), hardcoded table names (breaks DAG), everything-ephemeral (undebuggable), untested marts (silent grain drift), business logic in staging, circular jinja complexity, and no CI so main is perpetually broken.

questions.q: How do you do code review for dbt PRs — what do you look for?
questions.a: dbt PR review checklist: correct layer and naming, grain declared and tested, ref/source discipline, incremental logic handles late data, tests on new keys/joins (relationships), YAML docs updated, compiled SQL sanity (no accidental cross joins), and slim CI green.

questions.q: How do you backfill historical data through an incremental dbt model safely?
questions.a: Backfill safely: for date-partitioned incrementals use vars (--vars '{start: ..., end: ...}') driving the incremental predicate to reprocess a window, run in batches, verify with reconciliation queries; if logic changed historically, prefer --full-refresh in off-peak with the table swap pattern for zero downtime.

questions.q: How do you handle multiple environments/databases in one project (custom schemas, generate_schema_name macro)?
questions.a: Multiple environments: profiles/targets set database per environment; generate_schema_name macro controls schema naming (dev_username schemas for developers, clean names in prod); CI builds into ephemeral schemas dropped after; environment-specific behavior via target.name conditionals kept minimal.

questions.q: What are on-run-end results and artifacts (manifest.json, run_results.json) and what can you build with them?
questions.a: Artifacts: manifest.json (full DAG, configs — powers state selection and lineage tooling), run_results.json (per-model status/timing — powers observability dashboards and alerting), catalog.json (docs). on-run-end contexts can log results to warehouse tables for run-history analytics.

questions.q: How do you monitor dbt in production (logging, alerting on test failures, freshness SLAs)?
questions.a: Production monitoring: parse run_results into a run-history table (model durations, failures, test results), alert on errored builds and failed error-severity tests via the orchestrator, track freshness SLAs with source freshness checks, and watch duration trends to catch degrading models before SLAs break.

questions.q: What is unit testing in dbt (dbt unit tests) and how does it differ from data tests?
questions.a: dbt unit tests define given-inputs/expect-output fixtures in YAML, testing model logic on mock data at compile-time — verifying transformations before touching real data. Data tests validate actual warehouse contents post-build. Unit tests catch logic bugs; data tests catch data bugs.

questions.q: How would you introduce dbt into a team currently using stored procedures — migration and adoption strategy?
questions.a: Migration from stored procedures: inventory and rank procedures by criticality; carve out lineage into staged models (staging → intermediate → mart) rather than 1:1 translation; parallel-run with reconciliation tests; train the team on Git/PR workflow; migrate consumers gradually; retire procedures with celebration — adoption is as much cultural as technical.

questions.q: How do you document and enforce style (SQLFluff, formatting standards, PR templates)?
questions.a: Style enforcement: SQLFluff with dbt templater in pre-commit and CI (naming, keywords, indentation), a documented style guide (CTE-first, one model one purpose, explicit casts), PR templates with checklists, and codegen for consistent scaffolding — consistency makes a large project navigable.

questions.q: Design a dbt project for a freight/logistics mart: sources, staging, dimensional models, tests, and exposures for Power BI.
questions.a: Freight mart design: sources for booking/shipment/invoice systems with freshness checks; staging per source standardizing charge codes and units; intermediates resolving shipment lifecycle and charge allocation (FCL/LCL, TEU/CBM normalization); dim_customer, dim_lane, dim_charge_type, fct_shipment_charges at charge-line grain with unique tests; exposures declaring the Power BI revenue model.

questions.q: A nightly dbt build failed at 3 AM on a relationships test. Walk through triage: identify the model, inspect failures, decide warn vs block, and prevent recurrence.
questions.a: Triage at 3 AM: run_results identifies the failing test and model; query the stored failures/compiled test SQL to see offending rows; classify — upstream data issue (quarantine/fix source, rerun) vs logic bug (hotfix PR) vs legitimately evolving data (adjust test); decide severity policy; then post-incident: add an upstream source test or contract so the same break is caught earlier next time.

questions.q: What is Apache Airflow and what problems does an orchestrator solve beyond cron?
questions.a: Airflow is a platform to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor workflows as Python-defined DAGs. Beyond cron: dependency management between tasks, retries, backfills, SLA tracking, a UI with run history and logs, alerting, parameterization, and horizontal scaling of execution.

questions.q: Explain Airflow's architecture: scheduler, webserver, metadata database, executor, workers, triggerer.
questions.a: The scheduler parses DAGs and queues due task instances; the webserver serves the UI/API; the metadata database stores DAG/task state (source of truth); the executor dispatches tasks to workers (local process, Celery queue, or Kubernetes pods); the triggerer runs deferred (async) operators' waiting loops efficiently.

questions.q: What is a DAG? How do you define one in Python (context manager, @dag decorator)?
questions.a: A DAG is a directed acyclic graph of tasks with a schedule. Define via context manager: with DAG(dag_id='daily_load', schedule='@daily', start_date=..., catchup=False) as dag: — or the @dag decorator on a function containing @task-decorated tasks (TaskFlow style).

questions.q: What are operators, sensors, and hooks? How do they differ?
questions.a: Operators encapsulate one unit of work (BashOperator, PythonOperator, DatabricksRunNowOperator); sensors wait for a condition (file exists, task in another DAG done, API ready); hooks are the reusable connection clients operators use to talk to external systems (credentials from Connections).

questions.q: What is the TaskFlow API (@task) and how does it change passing data between tasks?
questions.a: TaskFlow defines tasks as decorated Python functions; return values pass automatically between tasks via XCom with dependency edges inferred from function calls — less boilerplate than PythonOperator + manual xcom_push/pull for Python-centric DAGs.

questions.q: What are XComs, what are they for, and why shouldn't you pass large data through them?
questions.a: XComs are small key-value messages between tasks stored in the metadata DB — task A pushes a filename or row count, task B pulls it. Not for data: the DB bloats and payload limits break; pass references (paths, table names, run IDs) and keep data in storage systems.

questions.q: How do you set task dependencies (>>, <<, chain, cross_downstream)?
questions.a: Dependencies: t1 >> t2 (t2 after t1), t2 << t1 equivalently; lists for fan-out/in (t1 >> [t2, t3] >> t4); chain() for linear sequences; cross_downstream() for many-to-many meshes. TaskFlow infers edges from data flow.

questions.q: Explain schedule intervals, logical (execution) date, and data intervals — why does a daily DAG run 'one day behind'?
questions.a: A run for interval [logical_date, logical_date + interval) starts after the interval ends — the run 'for Monday' executes Tuesday 00:00, because Monday's data is only complete then. logical_date (execution_date) identifies the data interval being processed, not the wall-clock trigger time — the classic Airflow mental-model hurdle.

questions.q: What are catchup and backfill? When do you disable catchup, and how do you run a controlled backfill?
questions.a: Catchup auto-creates runs for every missed interval between start_date and now — disable (catchup=False) for jobs where only 'latest' matters. Backfill deliberately runs historical intervals (airflow dags backfill -s -e), relying on tasks being parameterized by data interval and idempotent.

questions.q: What is idempotency in the context of Airflow tasks and why is it non-negotiable?
questions.a: An idempotent task produces the same end state no matter how many times it runs for the same interval — delete-insert its partition, MERGE by keys, overwrite its output file. Non-negotiable because retries, backfills, and manual reruns are routine; without idempotency every recovery duplicates data.

questions.q: How do retries, retry_delay, exponential backoff, and SLAs work?
questions.a: retries + retry_delay (with retry_exponential_backoff and max_delay) re-attempt failed tasks — absorbing transient failures (network, spot eviction). SLAs flag tasks exceeding expected duration triggering callbacks/alerts — detecting slowness, not just failure.

questions.q: What are trigger rules (all_success, one_failed, all_done, none_failed_min_one_success) and use cases for each?
questions.a: Trigger rules govern when a task runs given upstream states: all_success (default), one_failed (react to any failure — cleanup/alert), all_done (run regardless — teardown), none_failed_min_one_success (join after branching where skipped is acceptable). They enable failure handling and branch joins.

questions.q: How do you implement branching (BranchPythonOperator / @task.branch)?
questions.a: @task.branch (BranchPythonOperator) returns the task_id(s) to follow; unselected branches are skipped. Use for conditional paths — full vs incremental load by date, weekday vs weekend logic — pairing the join task with none_failed_min_one_success so skips don't block it.

questions.q: What are Airflow variables and connections, and how do you manage secrets (secrets backends, Key Vault)?
questions.a: Variables are global key-values for config; Connections store credentials/endpoints centrally (encrypted, referenced by conn_id). Back both with a secrets backend (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) so secrets live in the vault, never in code or the metadata DB unencrypted.

questions.q: How do you parameterize DAG runs (params, dag_run.conf, templating)?
questions.a: params define per-DAG defaults overridable at trigger time (validated, templated); dag_run.conf carries arbitrary JSON passed when triggering (API/UI) — read via context or templates. Together they let one DAG serve ad-hoc reprocessing with custom dates or scopes.

questions.q: What is Jinja templating in Airflow and what are commonly templated fields ({{ ds }}, {{ data_interval_start }})?
questions.a: Templated fields render Jinja before execution with context: {{ ds }} (interval start date), {{ data_interval_start/end }}, {{ params.x }}, macros for date math. Operators template specific fields (bash_command, sql) — enabling interval-aware SQL and paths without Python glue.

questions.q: What executors exist (Sequential, Local, Celery, Kubernetes) and how do you choose?
questions.a: SequentialExecutor: single task at a time (dev only). LocalExecutor: parallel processes on one machine — small deployments. CeleryExecutor: distributed workers via a broker — classic scale-out. KubernetesExecutor: a pod per task — elastic isolation, per-task resources/images. Choose by scale, isolation needs, and ops maturity.

questions.q: What are pools, priority weights, and concurrency controls (max_active_runs, max_active_tasks, task concurrency)?
questions.a: Pools cap concurrent tasks sharing a resource (e.g., 5 slots for the warehouse); priority_weight orders queued tasks; max_active_runs limits simultaneous DAG runs; max_active_tasks caps per-DAG concurrency; task-level concurrency limits a single task across runs — collectively preventing resource stampedes.

questions.q: What are sensors' modes (poke vs reschedule) and deferrable operators — why do deferrables save resources?
questions.a: Poke mode holds a worker slot while sleeping between checks (wasteful for long waits); reschedule frees the slot between pokes. Deferrable operators go further: they suspend to the triggerer's async event loop, occupying no worker at all while waiting — the efficient default for long waits on modern Airflow.

questions.q: What are datasets / data-aware scheduling — triggering DAGs when upstream data updates rather than by time?
questions.a: Datasets (assets) let a producer task declare outputs and consumer DAGs schedule on dataset updates instead of time — 'run when upstream data actually landed'. This replaces fragile time-offset scheduling and ExternalTaskSensors for data-driven dependencies.

questions.q: How do you create dynamic tasks with dynamic task mapping (expand/partial)?
questions.a: Dynamic task mapping creates task instances at runtime from data: process = transform.expand(file=list_files()) spawns one mapped task per file with partial() for fixed arguments — parallel fan-out sized by actual workload, visible individually in the UI.

questions.q: What is the difference between dynamic task mapping and generating DAGs dynamically from config?
questions.a: Dynamic task mapping varies task count per run from runtime data (files arrived today). Dynamically generating DAGs (loops over config creating DAG objects at parse time) varies structure per deployment — config-driven pipelines for many similar sources. Mapping is runtime; generation is parse-time.

questions.q: How do you structure a repository of DAGs for a team (folder layout, shared libs, avoiding top-level heavy code)?
questions.a: Repository layout: dags/ thin DAG definitions only, plugins or a proper installed package for shared operators/logic, separate requirements management, tests/ mirroring structure, per-environment config. Keep business logic out of DAG files — import it — so it's testable without Airflow.

questions.q: Why is heavy computation in DAG-definition (top-level) code a problem for the scheduler?
questions.a: The scheduler re-parses DAG files continuously; top-level code (API calls, DB queries, heavy imports) runs on every parse, throttling scheduling for the entire deployment. Keep module level to lightweight definitions; do work inside task callables; cache expensive dynamic config.

questions.q: How do you test DAGs (dag.test(), unit-testing task callables, DAG integrity tests in CI)?
questions.a: Testing layers: dag.test() executes a full DAG locally in-process for fast iteration; unit-test task callables as plain functions with mocks; DAG integrity tests in CI (import all DAGs, assert no cycles, required defaults like owner/retries, parse time budget) prevent broken deploys.

questions.q: How do you deploy DAGs (git-sync, CI/CD pipelines, environments) and manage Airflow upgrades?
questions.a: Deploy DAGs via CI/CD: merge to main triggers sync to the environment's DAG storage (git-sync sidecar, baked images, or managed-service buckets) after tests pass; environments get branches/directories; Airflow upgrades tested in staging with provider pinning — DAGs are software artifacts, not files edited on servers.

questions.q: How do you monitor Airflow (task logs, Grafana/StatsD metrics, alerting via callbacks, on_failure_callback)?
questions.a: Monitoring: task logs (remote logging to blob storage), metrics via StatsD/OpenTelemetry into Prometheus/Grafana (scheduler heartbeat, queue depth, task durations, DAG parse time), plus callbacks (on_failure_callback, SLA callbacks) driving alerts — watch platform health and pipeline outcomes separately.

questions.q: How do you implement alerting to Slack/Teams/email on failures?
questions.a: Failure alerting: on_failure_callback posting to Slack/Teams webhooks with task, run, log link; email_on_failure for simple setups; route by severity (critical DAGs page, others post to channel); include data-interval context so responders know what to rerun.

questions.q: What happens when the scheduler goes down mid-run? How does Airflow recover state?
questions.a: Task state lives in the metadata DB, so a scheduler restart resumes cleanly: running tasks continue (executor-dependent), queued work re-dispatches, and missed schedules are picked up. HA schedulers (multiple instances) remove the single point of failure.

questions.q: What are zombie and orphaned tasks?
questions.a: Zombies are tasks the DB thinks are running but whose process died without reporting (worker crash) — detected by missed heartbeats and failed/retried. Orphaned instances lost their supervising job. Both are recovered by scheduler cleanup; frequent zombies signal worker instability or resource exhaustion.

questions.q: How do you handle long-running tasks vs Airflow's role as an orchestrator (submit-and-poll pattern, not doing the work in Airflow)?
questions.a: Airflow orchestrates; heavy compute belongs on external engines. Pattern: submit work to Databricks/Spark/warehouse, then wait via deferrable polling — not running the transformation in the Airflow worker. Workers doing data processing couple pipeline scale to Airflow infrastructure and starve the scheduler.

questions.q: How do you orchestrate Databricks from Airflow (Databricks operators, jobs API) and what are best practices?
questions.a: Databricks orchestration: DatabricksRunNowOperator triggers predefined Jobs (preferred — job config lives in Databricks/bundles), DatabricksSubmitRunOperator submits ad-hoc runs; deferrable versions poll without workers; pass parameters per data interval; let Databricks own cluster config, Airflow own cross-system sequencing.

questions.q: How do you orchestrate dbt from Airflow (BashOperator vs Cosmos vs dbt Cloud operator) — trade-offs?
questions.a: dbt orchestration options: BashOperator running dbt build (simple, one opaque task), Cosmos (renders each dbt model as an Airflow task with per-model retries/visibility), or dbt Cloud operator (triggers Cloud jobs via API). Cosmos for granular observability; Bash for simplicity; Cloud operator when dbt Cloud owns execution.

questions.q: How do you run containerized tasks (DockerOperator, KubernetesPodOperator) and why isolate dependencies?
questions.a: DockerOperator/KubernetesPodOperator run tasks in containers with their own images — isolating conflicting Python dependencies per task, packaging non-Python tools, and giving per-task resource requests. The standard cure for 'this task needs pandas 2, that one needs 1.5'.

questions.q: How do you pass artifacts between tasks properly (external storage + references, not XCom payloads)?
questions.a: Pass artifacts by reference: write outputs to object storage/tables with interval-scoped deterministic paths (or push the path via XCom), downstream reads the reference. XCom carries coordinates, storage carries data — keeping the metadata DB lean and tasks replayable.

questions.q: How do you design a DAG for a multi-source daily warehouse load with mixed dependencies and per-source failure isolation?
questions.a: Multi-source design: one mapped/generated ingestion task group per source (isolated failures — one source failing doesn't block others), a join with none_failed_min_one_success or per-source datasets, transformation triggered on required sources' completion, per-source retries/alerts, and clear reprocessing per source via params.

questions.q: What is the difference between depends_on_past and wait_for_downstream, and when are they needed?
questions.a: depends_on_past blocks a task until its own previous-run instance succeeded — for cumulative/sequential loads. wait_for_downstream additionally requires the previous run's immediate downstream tasks done — stronger serialization. Both can silently stall DAGs after one failure; use sparingly and alert on stalls.

questions.q: How do you version and evolve a DAG safely when task IDs or schedules change?
questions.a: Evolving DAGs safely: changing a schedule affects future intervals (mind catchup); renaming task_ids orphans history (old instances no longer match); removing tasks loses their lineage. Prefer additive changes, keep task_ids stable, version significant rewrites as a new dag_id with a cutover, and document run semantics changes.

questions.q: How do you implement cross-DAG dependencies (TriggerDagRunOperator, ExternalTaskSensor, datasets) and which do you prefer?
questions.a: Cross-DAG options: TriggerDagRunOperator (push — parent explicitly triggers child, passing conf), ExternalTaskSensor (pull — child waits on parent's task/interval alignment, fragile with schedule mismatches), datasets (data-driven — child runs when the dataset updates). Prefer datasets for data dependencies; TriggerDagRun for command-style invocation.

questions.q: What are common anti-patterns in Airflow (hardcoded dates, non-idempotent tasks, XCom abuse, monolithic DAGs)?
questions.a: Anti-patterns: non-idempotent tasks (retries corrupt data), datetime.now() instead of interval dates (backfills break), XCom as a data bus, heavy top-level DAG code, monolithic single-task DAGs (no retry granularity), sensors in poke mode for hours, hardcoded credentials, and catchup=True surprises flooding runs on deploy.

questions.q: How do managed offerings differ (MWAA, Cloud Composer, Astronomer) from self-hosting? What about Azure Data Factory as the 'similar tool'?
questions.a: Managed Airflow (MWAA, Cloud Composer, Astronomer) removes infrastructure ops (scheduler HA, upgrades, scaling) at higher cost and some version/config lag. ADF is a different paradigm: visual, connector-rich, Azure-native — 'similar tool' as scheduler/orchestrator but weaker as code, testing, and dynamic workflows.

questions.q: Compare Airflow to ADF/Fabric pipelines for orchestration — when would you pick each in an Azure shop?
questions.a: In an Azure shop: ADF/Fabric pipelines win for connector-driven ingestion, managed simplicity, gateway access to on-prem, and low-code teams. Airflow wins for complex Python-defined dependencies, dynamic fan-out, cross-platform orchestration (Databricks + dbt + APIs + non-Azure), and software-engineering workflow (tests, PRs). Many estates run both: ADF ingests, Airflow orchestrates the analytical DAG.

questions.q: Compare Airflow with newer orchestrators (Dagster, Prefect) at a concept level — assets vs tasks.
questions.a: Dagster centers software-defined assets (declare the tables/files you produce; orchestration derives from asset lineage) with strong typing/testing; Prefect emphasizes dynamic Pythonic flows with minimal boilerplate. Airflow remains the ecosystem/operator standard, converging on their ideas via datasets and versioned DAGs.

questions.q: What changed conceptually in Airflow 2.x → 3.x that you're aware of (API-based task execution, UI, versioned DAGs)?
questions.a: Airflow 3 headlines: DAG versioning (runs remember the code version that produced them), a rebuilt UI, task execution via a stable Task API enabling remote/edge workers and stronger isolation, scheduler-driven backfills, and removal of legacy paths (SubDAGs, direct DB access from workers).

questions.q: How do you secure Airflow (RBAC, roles, restricting connections editing, audit)?
questions.a: Securing Airflow: RBAC roles scoping UI/API access, secrets in an external backend not the metadata DB, restricting connection edit rights, remote logs with access control, network isolation for the webserver, audit logs for admin actions, and no credentials in DAG code or Variables plaintext.

questions.q: How do you implement a 'rerun from failure point' operationally (clearing task instances, downstream/upstream clearing)?
questions.a: Rerun from failure: clear the failed task instance (with downstream) so the scheduler re-executes just that subtree for the interval — idempotent tasks make this safe; 'Clear' with upstream/downstream/future flags controls scope. This surgical recovery is a core reason task granularity matters.

questions.q: How do you handle timezone-aware scheduling correctly?
questions.a: Schedules honor the DAG's timezone if start_date is timezone-aware (pendulum.timezone('Asia/Dubai')) — cron fires in that zone including DST shifts; internally Airflow stores UTC. Never mix naive datetimes; explicitly choose whether business schedules follow local civil time or UTC.

questions.q: How do you throttle calls to a rate-limited API across many mapped tasks (pools, concurrency)?
questions.a: Throttle API-bound mapped tasks with a dedicated pool sized to the rate limit (e.g., 3 slots), optionally max_active_tis_per_dag on the mapped task, client-side rate limiting/backoff inside the callable honoring Retry-After — pool caps concurrency, code handles per-call pacing.

questions.q: Design an orchestration for: ingest 20 sources hourly, run dbt on completion of all, refresh a Power BI dataset, and alert on any SLA breach.
questions.a: Design: 20 mapped/generated ingestion task groups (per-source isolation, retries, dataset outputs) on an hourly schedule; dbt build triggered by dataset completion of all sources (or a join task with none_failed rule) running via Cosmos; on dbt success, a task calls the Power BI/Fabric API to refresh the dataset and polls completion; SLA callbacks and on_failure_callbacks route to Teams with run context; per-source reprocessing exposed via params.

questions.q: A daily DAG has been silently succeeding but loading zero rows for a week. What guardrails were missing, and how do you add them (row-count checks, data quality gates, anomaly alerts)?
questions.a: Missing guardrails: success meant 'task exited 0', not 'data arrived'. Add data-aware checks: post-load row-count/volume assertions vs expected ranges (fail the task on zero rows), source freshness checks before transforming, dbt tests gating downstream, anomaly alerts on volume trends, and dashboard-level freshness SLAs — redefining success as verified data, not exit codes.

questions.q: What is the difference between ETL and ELT, and why has ELT become dominant with cloud warehouses/lakehouses?
questions.a: ETL transforms before loading (external engine, e.g., Informatica/SSIS); ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse/lakehouse. ELT won because cloud engines scale transformation compute cheaply, raw retention enables reprocessing with new logic, and SQL/dbt-based transformation is more accessible and versionable.

questions.q: Explain medallion architecture (Bronze/Silver/Gold). What contracts and guarantees does each layer provide?
questions.a: Bronze: raw, append-only, source-faithful — the replayable system of record. Silver: cleaned, deduplicated, conformed types and keys — trustworthy entity-level data. Gold: business-level aggregates and dimensional models — consumption contracts. Each layer guarantees progressively stronger quality, letting consumers pick the right trust level and engineers reprocess from raw.

questions.q: What is idempotency in pipelines and what patterns achieve it (overwrite-by-partition, merge on keys, run IDs)?
questions.a: An idempotent pipeline yields the same end state however many times it runs for the same input window. Patterns: overwrite the target partition per run (replaceWhere), MERGE on business keys, delete-then-insert scoped to the load window, exactly-once file tracking (Auto Loader), and run-ID-keyed side effects. Idempotency turns retries and backfills from risks into routine.

questions.q: What is exactly-once vs at-least-once processing, and how do you achieve effective exactly-once in batch pipelines?
questions.a: At-least-once delivery means duplicates are possible; exactly-once means each record affects state once. In batch, achieve effective exactly-once by combining at-least-once execution with idempotent writes (MERGE by key, partition overwrite) — the transport may duplicate, but the sink converges.

questions.q: How do you design incremental loads: watermarks, CDC, change data feeds, and handling late-arriving data?
questions.a: Incremental design: track a high-water mark (max updated_at/ID) in a control table, extract rows beyond it, MERGE into the target, update the watermark transactionally on success. Handle late arrivals with a lookback window (reprocess last N days) or CDC; never trust event time alone for completeness.

questions.q: What is Change Data Capture (CDC)? Compare log-based CDC, trigger-based, and timestamp-based approaches.
questions.a: CDC captures source changes rather than re-extracting snapshots. Log-based (Debezium, native replication) reads the transaction log — low impact, complete, ordered; trigger-based writes change tables via triggers — invasive, adds load; timestamp-based queries modified_at — simple but misses hard deletes and untimestamped updates. Prefer log-based when available.

questions.q: How do you handle schema evolution and schema drift from sources without breaking downstream consumers?
questions.a: Handle schema drift by contract: additive columns flow through automatically (mergeSchema, rescued-data columns), breaking changes (drops/renames/type changes) are caught by schema validation at ingestion and quarantined pending review; versioned schemas and comms with source owners prevent silent breakage downstream.

questions.q: What are data contracts and how do they formalize producer/consumer expectations?
questions.a: Data contracts are explicit, machine-checkable agreements between producers and consumers: schema, types, constraints, semantics, SLAs, ownership. Enforced via schema registries, dbt model contracts, or CI checks — moving breakage detection from downstream dashboards to producer build time.

questions.q: What is data modeling for analytics: Kimball dimensional modeling vs Inmon vs Data Vault — when does each fit?
questions.a: Kimball: dimensional star schemas built incrementally per business process — the analytics default. Inmon: normalized enterprise warehouse first, marts derived — strong governance, heavier upfront. Data Vault: hubs/links/satellites for auditability and parallel loading in volatile multi-source environments — at query complexity cost. Most lakehouses run Kimball Gold over Vault-ish or raw Silver.

questions.q: Explain facts and dimensions, grain declaration, conformed dimensions, and why grain mistakes are the root of most BI bugs.
questions.a: Facts record measurable events at a declared grain; dimensions give descriptive context. Declaring grain ('one row per shipment charge line') is the single most important modeling act — aggregations, joins, and tests all depend on it. Conformed dimensions (shared dim_customer) make facts comparable across marts. Most BI bugs trace to undeclared or violated grain.

questions.q: How do you implement SCD Types 0/1/2/3 and choose between them?
questions.a: SCD0: never changes. SCD1: overwrite — no history, for corrections. SCD2: new row per change with effective dates/current flag — full history, the analytics default for slowly changing attributes. SCD3: previous-value columns — limited history for specific comparisons. Choose per attribute based on whether history has analytical value.

questions.q: What is the 'one big table' (OBT) approach vs star schema — trade-offs for modern engines and BI tools?
questions.a: OBT denormalizes everything into one wide table — simple for consumers and fast on columnar engines, but duplicates dimension updates, obscures grain, and bloats with many-to-many. Star schemas keep reusable conformed dimensions and clear grain. Pragmatic answer: star schema as the governed core; OBT views generated from it for specific consumers.

questions.q: What dimensions of data quality do you test (completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, timeliness, accuracy)?
questions.a: Quality dimensions: completeness (nulls, missing rows vs control totals), uniqueness (key duplicates), validity (domains, formats, ranges), consistency (cross-field and cross-system agreement), timeliness (freshness vs SLA), accuracy (agreement with reality — hardest, via reconciliation). Test each explicitly rather than assuming 'no errors = good data'.

questions.q: How do you implement data quality gates in pipelines (fail vs quarantine vs warn) and where in the flow?
questions.a: Place gates at layer boundaries: ingestion checks (schema, counts) before Bronze→Silver, business rules before Silver→Gold. Fail the pipeline for contract-critical breaches; quarantine bad rows and continue for isolated record issues (with counts alerted); warn for informational drift. Every gate logs metrics — silent gates are no gates.

questions.q: What tools/frameworks support data quality (Great Expectations, dbt tests, DLT expectations, custom asserts)?
questions.a: Frameworks: dbt tests (SQL assertions in the transformation DAG), Great Expectations/pandera (declarative suites for Python pipelines), DLT expectations (inline lakehouse enforcement), plus custom assert-and-log notebooks. Choose what lives closest to where the data is transformed so failures block promotion.

questions.q: What is data observability (freshness, volume, schema, lineage, distribution monitoring) and how does it differ from testing?
questions.a: Observability monitors data health continuously in production — freshness, volume anomalies, schema changes, distribution drift, lineage — typically via metadata rather than explicit rules (Monte Carlo-style). Testing asserts known expectations at build time; observability catches unknown-unknowns after deployment. Mature platforms need both.

questions.q: How do you design pipeline monitoring and alerting so on-call gets signal, not noise?
questions.a: Design alerting by severity and actionability: page only for consumer-impacting failures (SLA breach, prod pipeline down), route degradation warnings to channels, digest informational drift. Every alert needs an owner and a runbook link; alerts nobody acts on get deleted — alert fatigue is a reliability failure itself.

questions.q: What is data lineage and why does it matter for impact analysis and debugging?
questions.a: Lineage maps data flow from source to consumption at table/column level. It answers impact analysis ('what breaks if I change this column'), root-cause ('which upstream feed corrupted this KPI'), and compliance ('where does PII propagate'). Captured automatically by Unity Catalog/Purview/dbt, it turns tribal knowledge into queryable metadata.

questions.q: What is a data catalog and how do governance tools (Purview, Unity Catalog, Collibra, Informatica EDC/Axon) fit the stack?
questions.a: A catalog inventories datasets with ownership, descriptions, classifications, and lineage for discovery and governance. Purview scans and classifies the Azure estate; Unity Catalog governs the lakehouse natively; Collibra/Informatica EDC+Axon add enterprise stewardship workflows and business glossaries — the catalog is where trust and findability live.

questions.q: How do you handle PII: classification, masking, tokenization, encryption at rest/in transit, and right-to-be-forgotten?
questions.a: PII handling: classify at ingestion (tags/sensitivity labels), minimize collection, mask or tokenize in non-prod and analytics layers (dynamic masking, hashing with salt), encrypt at rest and in transit, restrict via column/row security, log access, and design deletion paths (right-to-be-forgotten) including time-travel/backup purge.

questions.q: What is the principle of least privilege applied to data platforms?
questions.a: Least privilege: every principal gets the minimum access to do its job — service principals scoped per pipeline to specific containers/schemas, analysts read Gold not Bronze, no shared admin accounts, time-boxed elevated access. Blast radius of any compromised credential stays small.

questions.q: How do you version control everything (SQL, notebooks, infra, configs) and why are notebooks-only workflows risky?
questions.a: Version control everything that defines the platform: SQL/dbt models, notebook source, pipeline definitions (as code/JSON), infra (Terraform/Bicep), configs, and even grants. Notebook-only workflows without Git mean no review, no rollback, no reproducibility — 'the pipeline is whatever is currently saved in prod' is an incident waiting.

questions.q: What does CI/CD look like for data pipelines — what do you actually test in CI?
questions.a: Data CI: lint (SQLFluff), unit tests on transformation logic with fixtures, DAG/import integrity, schema contract validation, and slim builds of changed models against a CI environment with tests. CD: automated deploy to staging, integration run on sample data, gated prod promotion. You test logic and contracts in CI; full-data validation happens post-deploy via monitoring.

questions.q: What is infrastructure as code (Terraform/Bicep) and why should data platforms be reproducible?
questions.a: IaC (Terraform/Bicep) declares workspaces, storage, clusters, and permissions as reviewed, versioned code — environments become reproducible (spin up identical test), auditable (who changed what), and recoverable (rebuild from code). Click-ops platforms drift and can't be trusted to match documentation.

questions.q: How do you manage environments (dev/test/prod) for data — including test data strategies and anonymization?
questions.a: Environment strategy: isolated dev/test/prod (separate workspaces/subscriptions), config-driven pointing (same code, different targets), prod-like test data via subsetted and anonymized copies or synthetic data — never raw PII in lower environments — and promotion only through CI/CD, never manual edits in prod.

questions.q: How do you make pipelines restartable and rerunnable safely after partial failure?
questions.a: Restartability: break pipelines into idempotent, individually rerunnable steps; persist state (watermarks, processed-file logs) transactionally with the data; make steps skip-if-done via run manifests; scope reruns to the failed step and interval rather than whole-pipeline replays. Test the restart path — an untested recovery procedure doesn't exist.

questions.q: What are backfills, how do you design for them from day one, and what makes them dangerous?
questions.a: Backfills reprocess history through current logic. Design for them upfront: parameterize every task by data interval, keep raw data (Bronze) forever-ish, make writes idempotent per interval, and throttle backfill parallelism. Dangers: overwhelming sources/warehouse, mixing logic versions across history, and triggering downstream side effects (emails, exports) for historical runs.

questions.q: How do you reconcile and validate data between source and target (row counts, hash totals, sampling, financial reconciliation)?
questions.a: Reconciliation levels: row counts per load window; hash/sum totals of measures (financial reconciliation to the cent for money data); distinct key counts; sampled row-level comparison; and EXCEPT-based exact diffs for certification. Automate as post-load assertions with logged results and thresholds — reconciliation is the proof your pipeline tells the truth.

questions.q: What is orchestration vs choreography (scheduler-driven vs event-driven pipelines)?
questions.a: Orchestration: a central scheduler (Airflow) explicitly sequences work — visible, controllable, single pane. Choreography: components react to events (file arrival, dataset updated) without a central brain — loosely coupled, scales organizationally, harder to trace end-to-end. Modern platforms blend: event-driven ingestion, orchestrated transformation.

questions.q: Batch vs streaming vs micro-batch: how do you choose based on latency requirements and cost?
questions.a: Choose by latency requirement honestly: batch (hours/daily) for most reporting — cheapest, simplest; micro-batch (minutes) when 'near-real-time' means minutes — Structured Streaming/frequent triggers; true streaming (seconds) only for operational use cases (alerting, tracking) that act on events immediately. Streaming's complexity and cost need a business case, not a fashion statement.

questions.q: What is the Lambda vs Kappa architecture debate, and how do lakehouses change it?
questions.a: Lambda ran parallel batch and speed layers (accurate + fast) at the cost of dual codebases; Kappa said stream everything, replaying the log for reprocessing. Lakehouses largely dissolve the debate: one Delta table serves batch and streaming reads/writes, and incremental engines (Structured Streaming, CDF) give Kappa-like unification with batch simplicity.

questions.q: What file formats do you choose and why (Parquet, Avro, ORC, JSON, CSV) — schema, splittability, compression?
questions.a: Parquet: columnar, compressed, splittable, schema-rich — the analytics default. Avro: row-based with strong schema evolution — streaming/Kafka and write-heavy landing. ORC: Parquet's Hive-world sibling. JSON: flexible interchange, expensive to scan — landing only. CSV: universal but schema-less and fragile — ingest, then convert. Choose columnar for reading, row for streaming/writing.

questions.q: Why do small files hurt distributed systems, and what compaction strategies exist?
questions.a: Every file carries per-task and per-metadata overhead: listings, open/close, scheduler tasks, memory for footers. Thousands of KB-sized files can make a small dataset slower than a huge one. Prevent via optimized writes and sensible partitioning; cure via compaction (OPTIMIZE, rewrite jobs) on a schedule tied to write patterns.

questions.q: How do you choose partitioning strategies for storage vs the anti-pattern of over-partitioning?
questions.a: Partition storage by the dominant filter with low-to-moderate cardinality — usually date — targeting partitions of at least hundreds of MB. Over-partitioning (by high-cardinality IDs or multi-column explosions) creates millions of tiny files and metadata pain. Modern alternative: liquid clustering/Z-order data skipping instead of physical partitions for secondary keys.

questions.q: What is late-binding vs early-binding of schema (schema-on-read vs schema-on-write)?
questions.a: Schema-on-write validates and types data at load (warehouses) — early failure, trustworthy reads. Schema-on-read applies schema at query time (lakes) — flexible landing, deferred pain. Lakehouse practice: schema-on-read at Bronze (accept everything, rescue anomalies), schema-on-write from Silver (Delta enforcement) — flexibility at the edge, contracts inside.

questions.q: How do you document a data platform so it survives team turnover (READMEs, ADRs, model docs, runbooks)?
questions.a: Documentation that survives turnover: READMEs per repo (purpose, setup, run), architecture decision records (why choices were made), model/column docs generated from code (dbt docs), runbooks per pipeline (failure modes, recovery steps), and ownership metadata in the catalog. Documentation adjacent to code stays alive; wikis rot.

questions.q: What are SLAs, SLOs, and SLIs for data products, and how do you measure pipeline reliability?
questions.a: SLA: the promise to consumers ('Gold refreshed by 07:00, 99.5% of days'). SLO: internal target backing it (pipeline completes by 06:30). SLI: the measured indicator (actual completion time, freshness lag, test pass rate). Measure and publish them — reliability becomes a managed number instead of vibes.

questions.q: How do you estimate and optimize cloud costs for data workloads (compute right-sizing, storage tiers, query patterns)?
questions.a: Cost optimization: right-size and auto-terminate compute, job-scoped clusters, spot for fault-tolerant batch, storage lifecycle tiers for cold data, prune unused pipelines and tables (usage telemetry), incremental over full recomputes, pushdown-friendly file layouts, and per-team cost attribution via tags — visibility first, then targeted fixes on the top spenders.

questions.q: What is DataOps and how does it borrow from DevOps?
questions.a: DataOps applies DevOps to data: version control, CI/CD, automated testing, monitoring, and collaborative ownership of the path from raw data to consumption — shortening cycle time from 'analyst asks' to 'trusted data ships' while raising reliability. Culture and process as much as tooling.

questions.q: What is a data mesh (domain ownership, data as a product, self-serve platform, federated governance) and what are its critiques?
questions.a: Data mesh: domains own their data as products (discoverable, documented, quality-assured), on a self-serve platform, under federated governance standards. Critiques: demands org maturity and duplicated skills in every domain, risks inconsistency without strong federation, and is overkill below a certain scale — many orgs need good central platform engineering, not mesh.

questions.q: What is the role of a metadata-driven / config-driven framework in scaling ingestion across hundreds of sources?
questions.a: Metadata-driven frameworks store source definitions (connection, object, watermark column, load type, targets) in control tables; generic parameterized pipelines loop the config. Onboarding source #200 is a config row plus tests, not new code — consistency, scale, and centralized fixes, at the cost of framework complexity to maintain.

questions.q: How do you handle secrets, keys, and service principals in pipelines securely?
questions.a: Secrets: store in a vault (Key Vault) referenced at runtime; prefer managed identities over static secrets entirely; scope service principals narrowly per pipeline; rotate on schedule; never in code, configs in Git, notebook outputs, or logs; scan repos for leaked credentials in CI.

questions.q: What is your approach to error handling: dead-letter queues, quarantine tables, retry policies, and poison messages?
questions.a: Error handling tiers: transient errors retry with backoff; malformed records route to dead-letter/quarantine tables with error context (never silently dropped, never blocking the batch); poison messages (repeatedly failing) get isolated and alerted after N attempts; systemic failures fail fast and page. Every path logs counts so error volume is itself monitored.

questions.q: How do you ensure ordering and deduplication when ingesting from message queues or APIs?
questions.a: Queue/API ingestion: dedupe on producer-provided IDs or content hashes into an idempotent sink (MERGE); tolerate out-of-order by processing on event time with lateness windows, not arrival order; track per-partition offsets/cursors transactionally with the data write so 'processed' and 'stored' can't diverge.

questions.q: How do you design an API ingestion pipeline (pagination, rate limits, incremental cursors, auth token refresh)?
questions.a: API ingestion design: incremental cursors (updated_since) persisted per entity; pagination loops honoring next tokens; retries with exponential backoff and jitter honoring 429/Retry-After; token refresh handling; response schema validation; raw payload landing to Bronze for replay; and rate budgeting so backfills don't exhaust quotas needed by daily loads.

questions.q: What is the difference between a data lake, data warehouse, and lakehouse — and is the distinction disappearing?
questions.a: A lake stores cheap raw files (flexible, ungoverned by default); a warehouse stores governed, performant relational data (rigid, historically expensive). The lakehouse gives warehouse semantics (ACID, SQL, governance) on lake storage via table formats (Delta/Iceberg). The distinction is genuinely collapsing — the battleground now is catalogs and engines, not storage paradigms.

questions.q: How do you performance-test a pipeline before production (volume testing, worst-case data, soak tests)?
questions.a: Pre-production performance testing: run with production-scale volumes (cloned or synthetic), worst-case shapes (skewed keys, wide rows, late data bursts), concurrent load (competing jobs, BI queries), and soak tests for streaming (hours, watching state growth and memory). Capacity headroom targets and degradation behavior get decided before go-live, not during the first month-end.

questions.q: What does 'shift-left data quality' mean?
questions.a: Shift-left quality: validate as close to the producer as possible — contracts and checks at ingestion rather than discovering breakage in dashboards. The earlier a defect is caught, the cheaper: a rejected file at landing costs minutes; a wrong executive KPI costs trust.

questions.q: How do you plan a migration/re-platforming (strangler pattern, parallel run, reconciliation, cutover criteria)?
questions.a: Migration playbook: inventory and prioritize by value/complexity; build the target landing zone and one thin end-to-end slice first (prove the path); strangler pattern — migrate pipeline by pipeline while legacy runs; parallel-run with automated reconciliation per migrated asset; define cutover criteria (N clean parallel days); keep rollback until stability; retire legacy explicitly with dates.

questions.q: Describe your framework for root-cause analysis when a stakeholder reports wrong numbers in a dashboard fed by a multi-hop pipeline.
questions.a: RCA framework: reproduce and scope the wrongness (which metric, since when, how big); trace lineage backwards layer by layer comparing values at each hop (Gold → Silver → Bronze → source) to localize the divergence point; identify the change that coincided (deploy, schema drift, data anomaly, logic edge case); fix forward with a test that would have caught it; write the postmortem — the goal is class-elimination, not just incident closure.

questions.q: Map the Azure data landscape: ADLS Gen2, ADF, Synapse, Databricks, Fabric, SQL Database, Event Hubs, Stream Analytics — what role does each play?
questions.a: ADLS Gen2: the lake storage foundation. ADF: ingestion/orchestration. Databricks: Spark lakehouse compute. Synapse: previous-gen integrated analytics (dedicated/serverless SQL + Spark). Fabric: the current SaaS unification (successor direction). Azure SQL family: operational databases. Event Hubs: streaming ingestion. Stream Analytics: SQL-on-streams. Together: sources → ingestion → lake → transform → serve → BI.

questions.q: What is ADLS Gen2 and how does hierarchical namespace differ from flat Blob storage? Why does it matter for analytics?
questions.a: ADLS Gen2 is Blob storage with hierarchical namespace: real directories with atomic renames and POSIX-style ACLs. Analytics engines need directory semantics (partition layouts, atomic commit protocols) — flat blob emulation of folders makes renames O(n) copies and breaks efficient partition operations.

questions.q: Explain storage account concepts: containers, access tiers (hot/cool/archive), redundancy options (LRS/ZRS/GRS/GZRS).
questions.a: Storage accounts contain containers (filesystems) holding blobs/files. Access tiers trade storage vs access cost: hot (frequent), cool (30+ days), cold/archive (rare, retrieval latency). Redundancy: LRS (3 copies, one datacenter), ZRS (across zones), GRS/GZRS (paired-region async copies) — choose per data criticality and DR requirements.

questions.q: How do you secure ADLS Gen2: RBAC vs ACLs vs SAS tokens vs access keys — and how do they interact?
questions.a: Security layers: Azure RBAC grants coarse roles at account/container scope (Storage Blob Data Reader/Contributor); ACLs refine per directory/file (POSIX rwx, default ACLs for inheritance); SAS tokens delegate scoped, time-boxed access; access keys are root credentials — disable or vault them. Evaluation: RBAC first, then ACLs; prefer identity-based (RBAC/ACL) over shared-key mechanisms.

questions.q: What are managed identities (system vs user-assigned) and why are they preferred over service principals with secrets?
questions.a: Managed identities are Azure-managed service principals bound to resources (ADF, Databricks connector, VMs) — no secrets to store, rotate, or leak; authentication happens via the platform. System-assigned lives with one resource; user-assigned is shareable across resources. Default to managed identity wherever the service supports it.

questions.q: What is a service principal and how does an app authenticate to Azure resources (Entra ID / OAuth)?
questions.a: A service principal is an application identity in Entra ID with a secret/certificate, granted roles like any user. Apps authenticate via OAuth client-credentials flow to get tokens for Azure resources. Use where managed identity isn't possible (external apps, some tools); scope narrowly and rotate credentials.

questions.q: What is Azure Key Vault and how do pipelines/notebooks retrieve secrets from it?
questions.a: Key Vault centrally stores secrets, keys, and certificates with access policies/RBAC and audit logs. ADF references vault secrets in linked services; Databricks uses AKV-backed secret scopes; apps fetch at runtime via managed identity — rotation happens in one place and nothing sensitive lives in code or configs.

questions.q: What is Azure Data Factory? Explain pipelines, activities, datasets, linked services, and triggers.
questions.a: ADF is Azure's data integration service: pipelines (orchestration containers) of activities (copy, transform, control flow), datasets (data shape references), linked services (connections), and triggers (schedule/tumbling/event). It moves and orchestrates; heavy transformation is delegated to compute (Databricks, SQL, data flows).

questions.q: What is an Integration Runtime (Azure IR, self-hosted IR, SSIS IR) and when do you need a self-hosted IR?
questions.a: Integration runtime is ADF's compute for connectivity: Azure IR for cloud-to-cloud (managed, serverless), self-hosted IR installed on your VMs for private network/on-prem sources (outbound-only connection — no inbound firewall holes), SSIS IR to lift-and-shift SSIS packages. Private sources = SHIR or managed VNet with private endpoints.

questions.q: How does the ADF Copy activity work (source/sink, staging, parallel copies, DIUs) and how do you tune it?
questions.a: Copy activity moves data source→sink with format conversion: parallel copies partition the read, DIUs scale cloud compute, staged copy bounces via blob when direct paths are unsupported or for PolyBase loading. Tune via partition options on the source, DIU/parallelism settings, and file sizing; watch the throughput metrics per run.

questions.q: How do you build metadata-driven ingestion in ADF (Lookup + ForEach + parameterized datasets)?
questions.a: Metadata-driven ADF: a control table lists sources/objects/watermarks; a Lookup activity reads it, ForEach iterates rows, and parameterized datasets/linked services execute generic copy logic per entry. Hundreds of tables ingest through one pipeline; onboarding is a config row — the standard enterprise ingestion pattern.

questions.q: What are ADF trigger types (schedule, tumbling window, event-based/storage events) and how do tumbling windows support backfills and dependencies?
questions.a: Schedule triggers fire on wall-clock cadence; tumbling window triggers fire per contiguous interval with state — supporting dependencies between windows, retries per window, and backfill of past windows (the batch-correctness choice); event triggers fire on blob arrival/deletion for event-driven ingestion. Windowed loads = tumbling; files landing = event.

questions.q: How do you implement incremental copy in ADF (watermark pattern, CDC connectors)?
questions.a: ADF incremental: persist a watermark (max modified date/ID) in a control table; pipeline reads old watermark, copies rows beyond it, updates watermark on success — all transactional in sequence. For supported sources, native CDC/incremental connectors in ADF handle change tracking without custom watermark logic.

questions.q: How do Mapping Data Flows in ADF work and when would you use them vs Databricks?
questions.a: Mapping Data Flows are visual Spark transformations ADF compiles and runs on managed clusters — joins, derived columns, SCD patterns without code. Use for low-code teams and moderate complexity; choose Databricks when you need full code control, testing, complex logic, or better price-performance at scale.

questions.q: How do you call Databricks notebooks/jobs from ADF and pass parameters both ways?
questions.a: ADF calls Databricks via Notebook/Jar/Python activities against a linked service (job clusters recommended): pass parameters as base parameters (read via dbutils.widgets), return values via dbutils.notebook.exit captured in activity output. Modern alternative: trigger Databricks Workflows via REST/Jobs activity for richer job features.

questions.q: How does ADF handle errors: activity retry, failure paths, Until/If activities, and pipeline-level alerts?
questions.a: ADF error handling: per-activity retry counts/intervals for transient issues; failure dependency paths (red arrows) route to cleanup/notification activities; If/Until implement conditional and polling logic; pipeline outcome alerts via Azure Monitor or a dedicated notification pipeline (Logic App/webhook for Teams).

questions.q: How do you do CI/CD for ADF (Git integration, ARM templates vs the new CI/CD flow, parameterizing linked services per environment)?
questions.a: ADF CI/CD: Git-integrated authoring (feature branches, PRs to main); publishing generates ARM templates — classic flow deploys ARM to test/prod with parameter overrides (linked service URLs, Key Vault references per environment); the newer npm-based build validates/exports without manual publish. Deploy via Azure DevOps pipelines with approvals.

questions.q: What is Azure Synapse Analytics? Differentiate dedicated SQL pools, serverless SQL pools, and Spark pools.
questions.a: Synapse bundles dedicated SQL pools (provisioned MPP warehouse), serverless SQL (pay-per-query over lake files), Spark pools, and pipelines in one workspace. Dedicated for reserved, tuned warehouse capacity; serverless for exploratory/lake queries; Spark for engineering — now largely succeeded by Fabric for new builds.

questions.q: How does a dedicated SQL pool distribute data (hash, round-robin, replicated) and why does distribution key choice matter?
questions.a: Dedicated pools shard data across 60 distributions: hash distribution co-locates rows by key (large facts — pick a high-cardinality, join-heavy, skew-free key), round-robin spreads evenly (staging), replicated copies small tables to every node (dimensions). Wrong distribution = data movement (shuffle) on every join — the #1 Synapse performance factor.

questions.q: When do you use Synapse serverless SQL over files vs loading into a database?
questions.a: Serverless SQL suits ad-hoc exploration of lake files, logical layers over curated Parquet/Delta (views for Power BI), and infrequent access patterns — zero infrastructure, per-TB-scanned pricing. Load into a database (dedicated/Fabric) when queries are frequent, latency-sensitive, or need warehouse features — repeated scans of large data get expensive.

questions.q: What is PolyBase / COPY INTO for loading data into Synapse?
questions.a: PolyBase and COPY INTO bulk-load external files into dedicated pools: COPY INTO is the simpler, recommended T-SQL (auth options, error handling, format flexibility); PolyBase uses external tables — both parallelize across distributions, vastly outperforming row-based inserts for lake-to-warehouse loading.

questions.q: How does Fabric relate to Synapse and ADF — what is Microsoft's direction and how do you advise a company choosing today?
questions.a: Fabric is the strategic successor: Synapse workloads map to Fabric equivalents (Warehouse, Spark, RTI) on OneLake with Power BI unified. Advice today: new greenfield analytics → Fabric (or Databricks for code-heavy estates); existing Synapse → plan gradual migration (shortcuts to existing ADLS ease it); ADF remains supported with Fabric pipelines as the evolution path.

questions.q: What is Azure SQL Database vs SQL Managed Instance vs SQL Server on VM — how do you choose?
questions.a: Azure SQL Database: PaaS single databases, auto-patched, elastic — default for new apps. Managed Instance: near-full SQL Server surface (cross-DB queries, SQL Agent, CLR) — lift-and-shift from on-prem. SQL on VM: full control including OS — only when you need features/licensing PaaS can't offer. Choose the most managed tier your compatibility allows.

questions.q: What are DTU vs vCore models, and what are elastic pools?
questions.a: DTU bundles compute/IO/memory into abstract units (simple, capped); vCore separates cores/memory/storage with reserved pricing and hybrid benefit (transparent, scalable — the modern default). Elastic pools share capacity across many variable-usage databases — cost-efficient for SaaS-style fleets of small DBs.

questions.q: What HA/DR options exist for Azure SQL (zone redundancy, failover groups, geo-replication, backups/PITR)?
questions.a: Azure SQL HA/DR: built-in local redundancy with automatic failover; zone redundancy spreads replicas across AZs; failover groups provide cross-region async replicas with listener endpoints (apps reconnect transparently); PITR backups (up to 35 days) plus long-term retention. Design to your RPO/RTO — zone for HA, geo for regional disaster.

questions.q: What is Azure Event Hubs vs Service Bus vs Event Grid — messaging patterns for data platforms?
questions.a: Event Hubs: high-throughput event streaming (Kafka-compatible) with partitioned consumers and retention — telemetry/log ingestion. Service Bus: enterprise messaging — queues/topics with transactions, ordering, dead-lettering — commands and workflows. Event Grid: lightweight pub/sub for discrete events (blob created) with push delivery — reactive automation. Streams vs messages vs events.

questions.q: How would you build a streaming ingestion path in Azure (Event Hubs → Stream Analytics/Databricks/Fabric RTI → serving)?
questions.a: Streaming path: producers → Event Hubs (partitioned buffer) → processing via Stream Analytics (SQL windows, simple), Databricks Structured Streaming (complex logic, Delta sinks), or Fabric Eventstream→Eventhouse (KQL analytics) → serve to real-time dashboards/alerts and land to the lakehouse for history. Choose the processor by logic complexity and team skills.

questions.q: What is Azure Stream Analytics and what are its windowing functions (tumbling, hopping, sliding, session)?
questions.a: Stream Analytics runs SQL over streams with temporal windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), hopping (fixed, overlapping), sliding (event-triggered continuous), session (activity-gap-based) — aggregating per device/key per window from Event Hubs/IoT Hub into sinks like Power BI, SQL, or storage.

questions.q: What are Azure Functions and Logic Apps, and where do they fit in data workflows (lightweight triggers, notifications, APIs)?
questions.a: Azure Functions: serverless code on triggers (HTTP, timer, blob, queue) — lightweight ingestion shims, API endpoints, event-driven glue. Logic Apps: visual workflow automation with hundreds of connectors — approvals, notifications, SaaS integration. In data platforms: Functions for custom event handling, Logic Apps for human/SaaS workflow edges around pipelines.

questions.q: What is Microsoft Purview and how does it deliver scanning, classification, lineage, and glossary across the estate?
questions.a: Purview provides estate-wide governance: automated scanning and classification (PII detection) across Azure/on-prem/M365, a searchable catalog with business glossary, lineage across ADF/Synapse/Power BI, sensitivity labels, and access policies — the compliance and discovery layer above individual services.

questions.q: How do private endpoints, VNets, and managed VNets secure data services? What is the problem with public endpoints?
questions.a: Private endpoints give services private IPs inside your VNet so traffic never crosses public internet; managed VNets (ADF/Synapse) isolate service compute with managed private endpoints to sources. Public endpoints expose services to internet-reachable attack surface — enterprise posture: private endpoints + disabled public access + firewall exceptions only where unavoidable.

questions.q: What is Azure Monitor / Log Analytics / KQL and how do you monitor ADF and Databricks with it?
questions.a: Azure Monitor collects platform metrics/logs; Log Analytics stores them queryable via KQL; diagnostic settings route ADF pipeline runs, Databricks logs, and SQL telemetry there. Build KQL alerts and workbooks: pipeline failure rates, activity durations, capacity trends — one query layer across the whole platform.

questions.q: How do you set up alerting on pipeline failures and cost anomalies in Azure?
questions.a: Alerting setup: ADF diagnostic logs to Log Analytics with KQL alert rules (failed pipeline runs by name/severity) → action groups (email, Teams webhook, PagerDuty); Cost Management budgets with threshold alerts and anomaly detection for spend spikes; metric alerts on capacity/DTU saturation before users feel it.

questions.q: How does Azure DevOps fit your workflow: repos, branching strategy, build/release pipelines, YAML pipelines for data projects?
questions.a: Azure DevOps for data teams: Repos with branch policies (PR reviews, build validation), Boards for work tracking, YAML Pipelines building/testing (lint, unit tests, dbt slim CI) and deploying (ARM/Bicep, Databricks bundles, ADF publishes) through environment stages with approvals — the delivery backbone for everything-as-code.

questions.q: How do you manage IaC for a data platform on Azure (Bicep/Terraform) — what resources do you template?
